pages.title: Welcome to Drivers Ed
pages.html:
Welcome to Drivers Ed.

You're about to do something most adults take for granted: become the person trusted to control a 4,000-pound machine in real traffic, at real speed, around real people. That's a serious responsibility — and an enormous freedom. We're glad you're starting here.

This is a fully online, self-paced Florida drivers education course. Every reading, every interactive activity, and every quiz lives inside Canvas. You can complete it at your own pace from any laptop, tablet, or phone — anywhere you have internet.

Why this course matters

Driver education exists for one reason: the data is unforgiving. Crashes are the leading cause of death for American teenagers. The first six months of solo driving are the riskiest of any driver's life — and they are also the months when most teen drivers have learned the rules but haven't yet built the experience and judgment that keep them out of trouble.

The whole point of this course is to compress some of that experience into structured learning. Every Florida law, every defensive driving habit, every scenario in the activities is here because real drivers have been killed or injured by not knowing it.

A required step toward a Florida driver's license

Completing an approved Driver Education Traffic Safety (DETS) course — this course — is a Florida FLHSMV requirement for first-time drivers under 18 before they can take the Class E knowledge exam and earn a learner's permit. You'll learn the full graduated licensing path in detail in Unit 5, but the short version: this course is the first official step on that path.

What we ask of you

Take it seriously. Read carefully. Don't skim. Don't skip ahead. The skills you build here directly affect whether the people in your car — and the people in the cars around you — make it home safely.

When you're ready, click Next below to learn how the course is structured.

pages.title: How This Course Works
pages.html:
How This Course Works

The course is built around five units. Each unit has multiple lessons, and every lesson follows the same simple rhythm.

The five units

  1. Unit 1 — The Driver's Mindset. What it really means to drive: defensive driving, the IPDE process, sharing the road with all vehicle types, speed and stopping distance, and pulling it all together.
  2. Unit 2 — The Language of the Road. Florida traffic signs, signals, pavement markings, work zones, school zones, right-of-way, complex intersections, and highway driving.
  3. Unit 3 — Vehicle Control and Handling. Vehicle systems, pre-drive checks, basic maneuvers, speed and stopping distances, adverse conditions, emergencies, maintenance, plus new lessons on parking and backing, night driving, seat belts, and what to do after a crash.
  4. Unit 4 — Alcohol, Drugs, and Impaired Driving. How alcohol and drugs affect driving, Florida's DUI laws and consequences, BAC science, peer pressure, and how to plan around impaired driving.
  5. Unit 5 — Sharing the Road and Florida's Licensing System. Pedestrians and cyclists, motorcycles, trucks and buses, distracted driving, aggressive driving, and Florida's Graduated Driver License system in depth.

The lesson pattern (this is the same in every lesson)

  1. Reading. The lesson's content, explained clearly with Florida-specific laws, statistics, and procedures. Take your time. The readings are designed to be read carefully, not skimmed.
  2. Interactive Activity. A hands-on scenario challenge that asks you to apply what you just read. Most activities present 6–8 real-world situations and ask you to pick the right response. At the end, you'll see a results screen — take a screenshot of it and upload it as your assignment.
  3. Knowledge Check Quiz. Five multiple-choice questions to confirm you understood the lesson. You get three attempts, and after each attempt you'll see explanations for the correct answers.

End-of-unit summative assessment

Each of the five units ends with a Summative Assessment — a longer quiz that covers everything in the unit. Treat these the way you would a real exam: review your notes, then take it once you feel ready.

Navigating in Canvas

  • Use the Modules view in the left-hand course navigation to see the whole course laid out unit by unit, lesson by lesson.
  • Each item has a checkmark you can click to mark it complete as you go.
  • The course is set up for sequential progress, which means you'll work through items in order. Don't worry — it just keeps you from accidentally skipping the reading and going straight to the quiz.
  • If you close the course mid-lesson, Canvas remembers where you left off. Come back later and pick up exactly where you stopped.

Pace yourself — but don't skip ahead

This is a self-paced course. You can move quickly when the material clicks, and slow down when it doesn't. But please don't try to skim five lessons in a row to "get through it." That's not how driving knowledge works — and that's not how the road gives you feedback. Spread it out, let it sink in, and come back fresh.

When you're ready, move to Grading & What's Expected.

pages.title: Grading & What's Expected
pages.html:
Grading & What's Expected

The course grade is built from three components — knowledge check quizzes, interactive activities, and unit summative assessments. None of them are surprises, and all of them are designed to confirm that you've actually learned the material, not just clicked through it.

Knowledge Check Quizzes

  • 5 points each.
  • 5 multiple-choice questions per quiz.
  • 3 attempts allowed. Canvas keeps your highest score.
  • Correct answers are revealed after each submission, with an explanation for each question.
  • If you miss questions on your first attempt, go back to the lesson reading, find what you missed, and try again. The point is to learn — not to guess.

Interactive Activities

  • Completion-based credit. Each activity has scenarios with feedback as you go. At the end you'll see a results screen with your score.
  • Take a screenshot of the results screen and upload it in the assignment. That's how we confirm you completed the activity.
  • The score on the activity itself doesn't determine the grade — credit is given for completing and submitting. But you'll get the most out of the course if you actually engage with the scenarios rather than guessing through them.

Unit Summative Assessments

  • 25 points each.
  • Cover everything from that unit's lessons.
  • You should be able to take these comfortably if you've worked through the unit's lessons in order.

The Final Exam

  • 40 multiple-choice questions on the content of this course, 1 point each.
  • 80% (32 of 40) to pass. 3 attempts allowed; your highest score is kept.
  • No time limit. Take as long as you need. Only 5 minutes of the course's 360 minutes of content time is credited to the final exam, so a careful, unhurried attempt costs you nothing.
  • Per-question feedback is shown after your last attempt.
  • It unlocks after you complete all of the lessons and pass all five unit summative assessments.

Important: this final exam is a test on what this course taught you. It is not the Florida Class E Knowledge Exam. That exam is a separate 50-question test (40 correct to pass) administered by FLHSMV, an authorized third-party administrator, or a DELAP school program when you apply for your learner's license. Passing this course qualifies you to take it — it does not replace it.

What's expected of you

  • Complete items in order. The course is set up so that each item builds on the previous one. Don't skip ahead.
  • Read carefully. The readings are short by college-textbook standards but dense with the details that come up on the course Final Exam, on the Florida Class E Knowledge Exam you take afterwards at FLHSMV, and in real driving.
  • Engage with the activities. Read each scenario, think about it, then choose. The point isn't a perfect score on the first try — it's building the kind of pattern-recognition you'll use behind the wheel.
  • Don't memorize for the quiz and forget tomorrow. The Florida road test, the permit exam, and (most importantly) real driving will all check whether the knowledge stuck.

A note on academic honesty

Don't have someone else take quizzes for you. Don't copy answers. The point isn't the grade in this course — the point is the knowledge that keeps you alive on the road. If you cheat your way through here, the road won't be fooled.

One more thing

This is a serious course about a serious subject. Every Florida statute, every procedure, every statistic in this course is here because real drivers — many of them teenagers — have been killed or injured by not knowing it. Take this course as seriously as the difference it can make.

Click Next to see Florida's driver's license requirements.

pages.title: Florida Driver's License Requirements
pages.html:
Florida Driver's License Requirements

You'll learn Florida's Graduated Driver License (GDL) system in depth in Unit 5. This page is the short version: what completing this course leads to, and the official Florida DHSMV path from "no license at all" to "fully licensed Class E driver."

Florida's Graduated Driver License (GDL) System — Overview

Florida, like every other U.S. state, uses a graduated licensing system. The idea is simple: new drivers don't start with full driving privileges. You earn them in stages as you build experience and demonstrate that you can handle the responsibility. Florida's GDL has three stages:

  1. Learner's License (also called the "Learner's Permit")
  2. Class E License with under-18 restrictions (16–17 years old)
  3. Unrestricted Class E License (at 18)

What completing this course leads to

This course (or an equivalent approved by Florida DHSMV) is a required step before you can apply for a Florida Learner's License. Specifically, every first-time driver under 18 in Florida must complete an approved Driver Education Traffic Safety (DETS) course before taking the Class E Knowledge Exam. A first-time applicant who is 18 or older completes the 4-hour Traffic Law and Substance Abuse Education (TLSAE) course instead (F.S. 322.095). The DETS requirement comes from F.S. 322.1615(1)(c), as amended by chapter 2025-104, Laws of Florida; FLHSMV requires a minimum of 6 hours and has applied it to under-18 applicants since August 1, 2025.

Florida-specific requirements at each stage

Stage 1 — Learner's License (minimum age 15)

  • Complete an approved Driver Education Traffic Safety (DETS) course (you're doing this now). Applicants 18 and older complete the TLSAE course instead.
  • Pass the Florida Class E Knowledge Exam — administered by FLHSMV, not by this course (50 questions, 40 correct to pass — covers signs, signals, rules, and safe driving practices).
  • Pass a vision and hearing test.
  • If under 18, a parent or guardian must sign the application.
  • Provide required identity documents per the Florida DHSMV checklist (proof of identity, Social Security number, two proofs of Florida residential address).

With a Learner's License you may only drive when accompanied by a licensed driver age 21 or older in the front passenger seat. For the first 3 months, daylight driving only. After that, you may drive until 10 p.m.

Stage 2 — Class E License with under-18 restrictions (age 16 or 17)

To upgrade from a Learner's License, you must:

  • Hold the Learner's License for at least 12 months with no moving traffic convictions — or 12 months with one moving conviction for which you elected traffic school and adjudication was withheld (F.S. 322.05(2)).
  • Complete at least 50 hours of supervised driving, including 10 hours at night. A parent or guardian certifies these hours.
  • Pass the Florida driving skills test (the "road test").

Once you have the Class E license, F.S. 322.16 still limits when you may drive unaccompanied:

  • 16-year-olds may not drive between 11:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m. unless accompanied by a licensed driver at least 21 years old, or driving directly to or from work (F.S. 322.16(2)).
  • 17-year-olds may not drive between 1:00 a.m. and 5:00 a.m. under the same two exceptions (F.S. 322.16(3)).
  • Florida sets no limit on the number of passengers a driver under 18 may carry — but every additional teen passenger raises crash risk, so this is worth a family rule.

Stage 3 — Unrestricted Class E License (age 18+)

At 18, the nighttime restrictions lift and you have a standard Florida Class E driver's license — provided you've kept a clean record.

Parent / guardian involvement

Florida law explicitly involves a parent or guardian for any minor driver. Your parent or guardian signs your application, certifies your supervised driving hours, and is legally co-responsible for any financial liability from a crash you cause while driving on their signature. They are part of this process by law and by design.

After completing this course: where to go

  1. Schedule your Class E Knowledge Exam with FLHSMV or an authorized third-party administrator (applicants under 18 may take it online in many cases). This is a separate exam from the test at the end of this course.
  2. Visit a Florida DHSMV office or Florida Tax Collector branch (most license services are handled by county Tax Collectors in Florida). Bring required identity documents, the application, parent/guardian signature, and proof of completing this course.
  3. Pass the vision and hearing test.
  4. If under 18, you'll be issued a Learner's License. If 18+, you may go straight to scheduling your road test if you haven't already.
  5. After your hold period and supervised driving hours: schedule and pass the road skills test to receive your Class E license (with nighttime restrictions until you turn 18).

Useful Florida resources

  • Florida DHSMV — flhsmv.gov — official source for license requirements, forms, and online services.
  • Florida Driver License Handbook — available free as PDF from the DHSMV site.
  • Your county Florida Tax Collector — most license transactions are handled at Tax Collector branches, not DMV offices. Find yours through the Florida Tax Collectors site or DHSMV office locator.

For everything else about Florida's GDL — including all of the rules, restrictions, and the full reasoning behind the staged approach — see Unit 5, Lesson 5.6: Florida's Graduated Driver License System.

pages.title: A Note to Parents & Guardians
pages.html:
A Note to Parents & Guardians

If your teen is taking this course, you're not just a signature on a form — you are the most important factor in whether they become a safe driver. Decades of research consistently show that parental supervision during the learning stage, plus consistent expectations and modeling, predict teen driving safety better than anything else.

What this course covers

This is a full Florida driver education course, organized into five units:

  • Unit 1: The Driver's Mindset — defensive driving, hazard recognition (the IPDE process), sharing the road, speed and stopping distance.
  • Unit 2: The Language of the Road — Florida traffic signs, signals, pavement markings, work zones, school zones, right-of-way, intersections, highway driving, plus railroad crossings.
  • Unit 3: Vehicle Control and Handling — vehicle systems, basic maneuvers, speed management, adverse conditions, emergencies, vehicle maintenance, parking, night driving, seat belts, and post-crash response.
  • Unit 4: Alcohol, Drugs, and Impaired Driving — how impairment affects driving, Florida DUI laws and consequences, BAC science, peer pressure and refusal strategies, alternatives to impaired driving.
  • Unit 5: Sharing the Road and Florida's Licensing System — pedestrians and cyclists, motorcycles, trucks and buses, distracted driving, aggressive driving, and the Florida GDL system in depth.

Each lesson uses the same rhythm: read, do an interactive activity, take a 5-question knowledge check quiz. Every unit ends with a summative assessment.

Florida's GDL Supervised Driving Requirement

Under Florida law, your teen must complete at least 50 hours of supervised driving — including at least 10 hours at night — before they can take the road test for a Class E license (which carries nighttime restrictions until age 18). You (or another licensed adult you authorize) supervise these hours and certify them when your teen applies.

This 50/10 requirement is not paperwork — it is the most important crash-prevention measure in the entire licensing system. Research from AAA and NHTSA consistently shows that the more supervised driving a teen does before solo driving, the lower their crash risk in the first year of solo driving.

Practical tips for supervising practice driving

  • Start in low-stakes environments. Empty parking lots, quiet residential streets, and slow rural roads come first. Build up to multi-lane roads, highways, night driving, and rain over weeks — not in one afternoon.
  • Set the agenda before you get in the car. Pick one or two skills to focus on per practice session: today, lane changes and merging; tomorrow, parallel parking; next week, all-way stops.
  • Narrate your own driving. When you drive with them, talk through what you're scanning for, why you're slowing down, what you're predicting from other drivers. Hazard perception is taught more than learned.
  • Stay calm — even when they make mistakes. Yelling at a new driver in an active traffic situation is dangerous and counterproductive. Pull over, take a breath, debrief calmly, then continue.
  • Insist on phones in the glove box. No texting, no scrolling, not even "just glancing" — for them or for you. Model it.
  • Make seat belts non-negotiable. For everyone, every trip, every time. Florida law makes you legally responsible for under-18 passengers, but the deeper point is what your teen sees you do.
  • Practice in all conditions. Night, rain, fog, parking lots, highways, school zones, construction zones. Most new drivers' first crashes happen in conditions they haven't practiced in.
  • Talk about what to do AFTER a crash. Lesson 3.10 covers this in detail. Make sure your teen has a plan: stop, check, call 911 if needed, don't admit fault, document everything.

The parent-teen driving conversation

The single most protective thing you can do, beyond practice itself, is to have explicit conversations about expectations:

  • About phones: Where will the phone be while driving? Is "Do Not Disturb While Driving" mode enabled?
  • About passengers: AAA research shows each additional teen passenger raises a teen driver's crash risk substantially. What's your family's rule for who can be in the car in the first year?
  • About alcohol and drugs: What's the no-questions-asked plan if your teen — or their friend driving them — has been drinking or using? Most families settle on something like, "Text me anytime, I will come get you, and we'll talk about it the next day instead of in the moment." Lesson 4.6 covers safe alternatives.
  • About night driving: Florida's GDL restricts when teens can drive at night, and there's a reason — about half of teen driving fatalities happen at night. What are your family's expectations within (and beyond) the legal limits?
  • About consequences: What happens if there's a speeding ticket? A crash? A violation of the family rules? Decide before you need to.

What Florida's GDL is really protecting against

The GDL system isn't paperwork or bureaucracy. It exists because the first 6–12 months of independent driving are when crash rates are highest for any driver in their entire life. The nighttime curfews, the 50-hour requirement, the passenger restrictions in some states — every piece of GDL was added because data showed it saved lives.

Florida's GDL has measurably reduced teen driver fatalities since it was strengthened. The system works with you, not around you. Use the staged privileges as natural conversation points: "Next month you can drive unaccompanied — let's talk about what changes and what doesn't."

One last thing

The single best predictor of a safe teen driver is a parent who took the time. Not perfect, not always patient — but engaged. The hours you spend in the passenger seat of a 16-year-old's first driving sessions are some of the most important hours of their entire driving life. Thank you for being here.

quizzes.title: Lesson 1.1: Knowledge Check — What Does It Really Mean to Drive?

questions.text: In Florida, driving is legally considered a:

answers.text: Constitutional right guaranteed to all citizens
Privilege that can be earned and revoked
answers.feedback: Correct! Driving is a privilege, not a right. Florida can grant, restrict, or revoke your license based on your behavior and compliance with traffic laws.

answers.text: Requirement once you turn 16
Right granted after passing a written test

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Driving is a privilege — not a right. Unlike constitutional rights, your driver's license can be taken away if you violate traffic laws or fail to meet requirements.

questions.text: According to NHTSA data, what percentage of crashes are caused by human error?

answers.text: About 60%
About 75%
About 94%
answers.feedback: Correct! Approximately 94% of serious crashes are caused by human error — including distracted driving, speeding, impairment, and poor decision-making. This is exactly why driver education matters.

answers.text: About 50%

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. The answer is approximately 94%. Nearly all serious crashes are caused by human error, which is why learning proper driving skills and decision-making is so critical.

questions.text: What does IPDE stand for in the context of driving?

answers.text: Inspect, Plan, Drive, Evaluate
Identify, Predict, Decide, Execute
answers.feedback: Correct! IPDE stands for Identify, Predict, Decide, Execute. This four-step mental process helps you continuously scan for and respond to hazards while driving.

answers.text: Indicate, Prepare, Drive, Exit
Inspect, Predict, Determine, Execute

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. IPDE stands for Identify, Predict, Decide, Execute. You'll learn this process in detail in Lesson 1.2 — it's the foundation of safe driving decision-making.

questions.text: Which of the following makes Florida's driving environment uniquely challenging?

answers.text: All roads have speed limits under 45 mph
There are no pedestrians or cyclists on roads
Tourist traffic, sudden storms, and diverse road users
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida's unique challenges include millions of tourist drivers unfamiliar with local roads, sudden afternoon thunderstorms, diverse road users (pedestrians, cyclists, scooters), and high-speed highways alongside residential areas.

answers.text: Florida has the lowest crash rate in the nation

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida's driving environment is uniquely challenging because of tourist traffic, sudden thunderstorms, diverse road users (pedestrians, cyclists, scooters, trucks), and a mix of high-speed highways and residential zones.

questions.text: What is the primary goal of defensive driving?

answers.text: To arrive at your destination as quickly as possible
To follow every traffic law perfectly at all times
To anticipate and respond to hazards to prevent crashes
answers.feedback: Correct! Defensive driving is about anticipating danger, recognizing hazards early, and making smart decisions to prevent crashes — even when other drivers make mistakes.

answers.text: To avoid getting pulled over by law enforcement

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. While following laws is important, the primary goal of defensive driving is to anticipate and respond to hazards proactively — preventing crashes before they happen, even when other drivers are making mistakes.

quizzes.title: Lesson 1.2: Knowledge Check — The IPDE Process

questions.text: Which phase of IPDE involves scanning your environment for potential hazards?

answers.text: Execute
Predict
Identify
answers.feedback: Correct! Identify is the first phase — scanning for anything that could affect your driving. This includes other vehicles, pedestrians, road conditions, signs, and signals.

answers.text: Decide

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. The Identify phase is all about scanning and seeing. It's the foundation of IPDE — you can't react to what you haven't seen.

questions.text:
You see a ball roll into the street from between parked cars. Using IPDE, what would the Predict phase tell you?

Scenario: Residential neighborhood, parked cars on both sides.

answers.text: Slow down immediately
A child may follow the ball into the street
answers.feedback: Correct! In the Predict phase, you ask "what could happen next?" A ball in the street is a classic cue that a child may follow it — one of the most important predictive connections in driving.

answers.text: Honk your horn
Change lanes to the left

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Predict is about anticipating what COULD happen. A ball near children almost always means a child might chase it. The other answer choices describe the Decide or Execute phases, not Predict.

questions.text: A driver who completes the IPDE cycle effectively will typically:

answers.text: Drive faster than other traffic
React to hazards only after they become emergencies
Anticipate hazards and respond before they become emergencies
answers.feedback: Correct! The whole point of IPDE is proactive, not reactive, driving. By identifying and predicting early, you respond before a hazard becomes a crisis — giving you more time and more options.

answers.text: Always drive at or below the speed limit

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. IPDE is about proactive driving — identifying hazards early and responding before they become emergencies. It's not about speed; it's about awareness and early action.

questions.text: Which IPDE phase involves choosing between changing speed, changing direction, or communicating?

answers.text: Identify
Predict
Decide
answers.feedback: Correct! The Decide phase is where you choose your response: change speed, change direction, communicate (horn, lights, signals), or a combination. The quality of this decision depends on good Identify and Predict work.

answers.text: Execute

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Decide is the phase where you choose your action. Your four basic options are: change speed, change direction, communicate, or a combination. Good decisions depend on early identification and accurate prediction.

questions.text: Why do expert drivers scan their mirrors every 5–8 seconds?

answers.text: It's required by Florida law
To maintain continuous situational awareness for the Identify phase of IPDE
answers.feedback: Correct! Frequent mirror checks are how expert drivers maintain the Identify phase continuously. Your environment changes every few seconds — what was safe 10 seconds ago may not be safe now.

answers.text: To check their appearance
To watch for police

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Regular mirror scanning maintains the Identify phase of IPDE. Your driving environment constantly changes — traffic, pedestrians, and conditions shift every few seconds. Frequent checks keep you aware.

quizzes.title: Lesson 1.3 Knowledge Check — Sharing the Road

questions.text: Florida's 3-foot passing law requires drivers to:

answers.text: Give cyclists 3 feet when they are on the sidewalk
Maintain at least 3 feet of clearance when passing a cyclist on the road
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.083(2) requires a driver overtaking a bicycle in the same travel lane to pass at a safe distance of not less than 3 feet. If you cannot give 3 feet safely, you must stay a safe distance behind until you can.

answers.text: Keep 3 feet from all parked cars
Stay 3 feet behind motorcycles at intersections

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The 3-foot rule is about passing a cyclist who is riding on the roadway, not about sidewalks, parked cars, or following distance. F.S. 316.083(2) requires at least 3 feet of clearance when you overtake a bicycle in the same travel lane.

questions.text: At an unmarked intersection (no painted crosswalk lines), pedestrians:

answers.text: Have no right-of-way and must wait for all cars to pass
Should only cross at traffic lights
Still must be yielded the right-of-way because every intersection has an implied crosswalk
answers.feedback: Correct. A crosswalk exists at every intersection where the sidewalk lines continue across the road, painted or not. Under F.S. 316.130 a driver must yield — slowing or stopping if needed — for a pedestrian in that crosswalk on the driver's half of the roadway, and must stop and remain stopped where a signal or signage so indicates.

answers.text: Must make eye contact with all drivers before crossing

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. An unmarked crosswalk is still a crosswalk. F.S. 316.130 requires the driver to yield to a pedestrian crossing there, and F.S. 316.130(15) requires every driver to use due care to avoid colliding with any pedestrian.

questions.text: The #1 cause of car-vs-motorcycle crashes is:

answers.text: Motorcyclists speeding
Motorcycles running red lights
A car turning left in front of an oncoming motorcycle
answers.feedback: Correct. The most common car-versus-motorcycle crash is a driver turning left across the path of an oncoming motorcycle. A motorcycle's narrow profile makes it easy to overlook and hard to judge for speed and distance, so look twice before every left turn.

answers.text: Motorcycles riding in blind spots

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The most common car-versus-motorcycle crash is a driver turning left in front of an oncoming motorcycle. Look twice for motorcycles before you turn left, and never assume a bike is farther away or slower than it looks.

questions.text: "Inattentional blindness" in the context of driving means:

answers.text: Being temporarily blinded by oncoming headlights
Your brain filtering out objects it's not expecting to see, like motorcycles
answers.feedback: Correct. Inattentional blindness is your brain filtering out what it is not expecting to see. Drivers scanning for cars can look straight at a motorcycle or cyclist and never register it — which is why you scan deliberately for smaller road users.

answers.text: Not being able to see at night
Forgetting to check your mirrors

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Inattentional blindness is not about darkness or glare. It is your brain filtering out objects it is not expecting — the reason drivers look right at a motorcycle and still pull out in front of it.

questions.text: Florida's Move Over law requires drivers to:

answers.text: Move over only for police vehicles
Move over one lane or slow down 20 mph below the posted speed for stopped emergency vehicles, tow trucks, and disabled vehicles
answers.feedback: Correct. Under F.S. 316.126(1)(b) the Move Over Law covers stopped emergency vehicles, sanitation vehicles, utility service vehicles, wreckers, road and bridge maintenance or construction vehicles, and — since January 1, 2024 — disabled vehicles displaying hazard lights, flares, or emergency signage, or with people visibly present. Vacate the closest lane if you can; if you cannot, slow to 20 mph below the posted limit (5 mph if the limit is 20 mph or less).

answers.text: Always drive in the left lane
Move over only on highways

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The Move Over Law is not limited to police and not limited to highways. F.S. 316.126(1)(b) covers emergency, sanitation, utility, wrecker, and road and bridge maintenance vehicles, plus disabled vehicles displaying hazard lights, flares, or signage or with people visibly present. Move over one lane, or slow to 20 mph below the posted limit when you cannot.

quizzes.title: Lesson 1.4 Knowledge Check — Big Vehicles

questions.text: Which No-Zone around a truck is the largest and most dangerous?

answers.text: Front No-Zone
Rear No-Zone
Left Side No-Zone
Right Side No-Zone
answers.feedback: Correct. The right-side No-Zone is the largest and most dangerous blind spot on a large truck, extending across more than one lane. If you cannot see the driver in the truck's side mirror, the driver cannot see you.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The right-side No-Zone is the largest blind spot on a large truck — it extends across more than one lane. The front, rear, and left side are also No-Zones, but the right side is the most dangerous place to linger.

questions.text: What is the minimum recommended following distance behind a large truck?

answers.text: 2 seconds
3 seconds
4 seconds
answers.feedback: Correct. Give a large truck at least 4 seconds of following distance. A loaded truck needs far more room to stop than a car, and sitting closer puts you inside its rear No-Zone where the driver cannot see you at all.

answers.text: 1 second

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Two or three seconds is the guidance for following a car in good conditions. Behind a large truck, give yourself at least 4 seconds — the truck's stopping distance is much longer and its rear blind spot is deep.

questions.text: On a two-lane road with no median, when a school bus stops with its red lights flashing and stop sign extended, which vehicles must stop?

answers.text: Only vehicles behind the bus
Only vehicles in the same lane as the bus
Traffic in BOTH directions must stop
answers.feedback: Correct. On a two-lane road, traffic in BOTH directions must stop and remain stopped until the bus withdraws its stop signal (F.S. 316.172(1)(a)). The only exception is a divided highway separated by an unpaved space of at least 5 feet, a raised median, or a physical barrier.

answers.text: No one needs to stop if no children are visible

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. On a two-lane road with no median, every driver in both directions must stop for a school bus displaying its stop signal — whether or not children are visible. Passing a stopped school bus carries a minimum $200 civil penalty and 4 points, and $400 if you pass on the side children enter and exit.

questions.text: When approaching a railroad crossing with flashing red lights and lowering gates, how far from the nearest rail must you stop?

answers.text: At least 5 feet
At least 15 feet
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.1575(1) requires you to stop within 50 feet but not less than 15 feet from the nearest rail, and to stay stopped until the tracks are clear and it is safe to proceed. Never drive through, around, or under a gate that is closed or moving.

answers.text: At least 50 feet
As close as possible to see the train

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Florida law sets a stopping window, not a minimum of 5 or 50 feet: stop within 50 feet but NOT LESS THAN 15 feet from the nearest rail (F.S. 316.1575(1)). Pulling closer to see the train puts your vehicle inside the train's overhang.

questions.text: A truck ahead of you swings left before making a right turn. You should:

answers.text: Quickly pass on the right while there's space
Stay back and give the truck room to complete its wide turn
answers.feedback: Correct. A large truck needs the extra room to swing wide for a right turn. Stay back and never move up on its right — that is exactly where the truck's trailer will sweep, and it is the truck's largest blind spot.

answers.text: Pull alongside the truck on the right
Honk to alert the truck driver

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. When a truck swings left before turning right, the space that opens on its right is a trap, not an opening. The trailer sweeps through it as the turn completes. Stay back and let the truck finish the turn.

quizzes.title: Lesson 1.5 Knowledge Check — Speed

questions.text: What is the statutory (default) speed limit in a Florida residential area when no sign is posted?

answers.text: 25 mph
30 mph
answers.feedback: Correct. Under F.S. 316.183(2) the default maximum is 30 mph in business or residence districts and 55 mph everywhere else. A county or municipality may lower a residence-district limit to 20 or 25 mph after an investigation, but it must post it.

answers.text: 35 mph
45 mph

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Florida's statutory default in a business or residence district is 30 mph (F.S. 316.183(2)). Local governments may post 20 or 25 mph in a residence district, but where nothing is posted, 30 mph is the limit.

questions.text: If you double your speed, what happens to your braking distance?

answers.text: It doubles
It triples
It quadruples (4x)
answers.feedback: Correct. Braking distance grows with the SQUARE of speed, so doubling your speed quadruples the distance your car needs to stop after the brakes are applied — and that is on top of the reaction distance you travel before you touch the pedal.

answers.text: It stays the same

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Braking distance grows with the square of speed. Double your speed and braking distance is about four times as long, not twice as long.

questions.text: According to Florida's Basic Speed Law, can you be ticketed for going under the posted speed limit?

answers.text: No — you can never get a ticket if you're under the limit
Yes — if you're driving too fast for current conditions like rain or fog
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.183(1) forbids driving faster than is reasonable and prudent for the conditions, whatever the posted number says. In heavy rain or fog you can be cited for speeding while travelling under the posted limit.

answers.text: Only in school zones
Only on highways

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The posted limit is a maximum for ideal conditions, not a guarantee. Under F.S. 316.183(1) you must never drive faster than is reasonable and prudent for the actual conditions, and F.S. 316.185 requires you to slow for special hazards.

questions.text: At 60 mph, approximately how far does your vehicle travel per second?

answers.text: 44 feet
66 feet
88 feet
answers.feedback: Correct. At 60 mph you cover 88 feet every second. A two-second glance at a phone carries you the better part of a football field with nobody watching the road.

answers.text: 110 feet

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. At 60 mph you travel 88 feet per second (60 miles per hour is 88 feet per second). That is why even a brief glance away from the road covers so much ground.

questions.text: Under Florida law, which of the following is true about street racing?

answers.text: It's only illegal if someone gets hurt
Only the drivers can be charged, not spectators
Both drivers and spectators can be cited — the driver criminally, the spectator with a noncriminal $400 infraction
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.191 reaches the crowd as well as the drivers. A driver faces a first-degree misdemeanor on a first violation — a $500 to $2,000 fine and a mandatory 1-year license revocation — and a spectator at a race, drag race, or street takeover commits a noncriminal traffic infraction punishable by a $400 fine.

answers.text: It's legal on private roads

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Florida's racing statute does not wait for an injury and does not stop at the drivers. Under F.S. 316.191 a first-violation driver faces a first-degree misdemeanor, a $500 to $2,000 fine, and a 1-year license revocation, and a spectator faces a noncriminal $400 infraction.

quizzes.title: Lesson 1.6 Knowledge Check — Putting It All Together

questions.text: Which Smith System principle tells you to look 12-15 seconds down the road?

answers.text: Get the Big Picture
Keep Your Eyes Moving
Aim High in Steering
answers.feedback: Correct. Aim High in Steering means looking 12 to 15 seconds ahead — roughly a block in the city or a quarter mile on the highway — so you see a developing problem while you still have time and space to respond.

answers.text: Leave Yourself an Out

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Aim High in Steering is the principle about where you look: 12 to 15 seconds down the road, not just at the bumper ahead. Getting the Big Picture, Keeping Your Eyes Moving, and Leaving Yourself an Out are the other Smith System habits.

questions.text: "Leave Yourself an Out" means:

answers.text: Always have an exit strategy when parking
Maintain a space cushion with escape routes
answers.feedback: Correct. Leaving yourself an out means keeping open space around your vehicle — especially ahead — so you always have somewhere to go when another driver makes a mistake.

answers.text: Keep your windows open
Always drive in the right lane

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Leave Yourself an Out is about space, not parking. Keep a cushion of open space around the car, and position yourself so you always have an escape path if the vehicle ahead stops suddenly.

questions.text: What is commentary driving?

answers.text: Listening to an instructor's commentary
Reading road signs out loud
Narrating your driving observations and decisions out loud to build habits
answers.feedback: Correct. Commentary driving means saying your observations and decisions out loud — 'brake lights three cars up, cover the brake' — which forces you to scan actively and turns deliberate searching into an automatic habit.

answers.text: Talking to passengers about traffic

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Commentary driving is you narrating what you see and what you plan to do about it. Speaking your scan out loud keeps your eyes moving and makes hazard perception a habit rather than an afterthought.

questions.text: When a car is tailgating you, the safest response is to:

answers.text: Brake hard to teach them a lesson
Speed up to create distance
Increase your front following distance so you can stop more gradually
answers.feedback: Correct. When someone tailgates you, add space in FRONT of your vehicle. The extra cushion lets you slow gradually instead of braking hard, which is what protects you from being rear-ended.

answers.text: Pull over immediately

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Brake-checking a tailgater invites the crash you are trying to avoid, and speeding up just moves the problem. Increase your own following distance so any stop you make can be gradual, and let the tailgater pass when it is safe.

questions.text: The "space cushion" concept refers to:

answers.text: The air between your car and the road
Open space maintained around your vehicle in all directions
answers.feedback: Correct. A space cushion is the open space you maintain on all sides of your vehicle. Space is time, and time is what lets you see, decide, and act before a hazard becomes a crash.

answers.text: The distance between parked cars
The gap between your car and the speed limit

questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The space cushion is the open area you keep around your car in every direction — front, back, and both sides — so that another driver's mistake does not become your collision.

quizzes.title: Unit 1 Summative Assessment

questions.text: What does the "P" in the IPDE Process stand for?

answers.text: Prepare
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Review Lesson 1.2 on the IPDE Process.

answers.text: Predict
answers.feedback: Correct! The P in IPDE stands for Predict - anticipating what other road users might do.

answers.text: Practice
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The IPDE Process uses Predict, not Practice.

answers.text: Proceed
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The fourth step is Execute, not Proceed.

questions.text: According to the Smith System, what does "Aim High in Steering" mean?

answers.text: Keep your steering wheel positioned high
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This refers to where you look, not steering wheel position.

answers.text: Look 12-15 seconds ahead in your target area
answers.feedback: Correct! Aim High means looking ahead 12-15 seconds to identify hazards early.

answers.text: Keep your speed high on the highway
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This has nothing to do with speed.

answers.text: Adjust your seat to the highest position
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This refers to visual scanning, not seat position.

questions.text: Florida's 3-foot law requires drivers to:

answers.text: Maintain 3 feet distance from the curb
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The 3-foot law protects vulnerable road users.

answers.text: Give at least 3 feet of clearance when passing a cyclist
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida law requires at least 3 feet of clearance when passing cyclists.

answers.text: Park at least 3 feet from a fire hydrant
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Fire hydrant parking requires 15 feet clearance.

answers.text: Stop 3 feet behind the stop line
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The 3-foot law specifically protects cyclists.

questions.text: The "No-Zone" refers to:

answers.text: Areas where parking is prohibited
answers.feedback: Incorrect. No-Zone is related to large vehicle blind spots.

answers.text: School zones where stopping is not allowed
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This refers to truck blind spots.

answers.text: Large blind spot areas around trucks and buses where they cannot see you
answers.feedback: Correct! No-Zones are the extensive blind spots around large vehicles.

answers.text: Construction zones where entry is restricted
answers.feedback: Incorrect. No-Zone specifically refers to blind spots.

questions.text: Florida's Move Over Law requires you to:

answers.text: Move over one lane when safe or slow down 20 MPH below speed limit when approaching emergency/service vehicles with lights flashing
answers.feedback: Correct! The Move Over Law protects emergency workers and service personnel.

answers.text: Move to the right lane for faster traffic
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This refers to emergency and service vehicles with lights.

answers.text: Pull over completely whenever you see any flashing lights
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You must move over or slow down, not necessarily stop.

answers.text: Change lanes away from motorcycles
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This specifically applies to emergency/service vehicles.

questions.text: Florida's Basic Speed Law states that:

answers.text: You can always drive at the posted speed limit
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You must adjust speed for conditions.

answers.text: You must drive at a speed that is reasonable and prudent based on current conditions
answers.feedback: Correct! Even if the speed limit is 55 MPH, you must slow down for rain, fog, or other hazards.

answers.text: The minimum speed is always 40 MPH on highways
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Minimum speeds vary and conditions may require slower speeds.

answers.text: New drivers must drive 10 MPH slower than the limit
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The Basic Speed Law applies to all drivers based on conditions.

questions.text: If you double your speed, your stopping distance:

answers.text: Doubles
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The relationship is exponential, not linear.

answers.text: Triples
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Review the physics of stopping distance.

answers.text: Quadruples (increases by 4 times)
answers.feedback: Correct! Due to kinetic energy physics, doubling speed quadruples stopping distance.

answers.text: Stays the same
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Higher speeds dramatically increase stopping distance.

questions.text: When a school bus stops with its red lights flashing and stop arm extended, you must:

answers.text: Slow down and proceed with caution
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You must stop completely.

answers.text: Stop at least 20 feet away and remain stopped until the bus resumes motion or the lights stop flashing
answers.feedback: Correct! This applies to traffic from both directions unless divided by a barrier.

answers.text: Stop only if children are visible
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You must stop regardless of whether children are visible.

answers.text: Pass quickly before children cross
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This is illegal and extremely dangerous.

questions.text: The recommended following distance using the "3-second rule" should be increased to 4+ seconds when:

answers.text: Driving on a sunny day with light traffic
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Ideal conditions allow for the standard 3 seconds.

answers.text: Driving in rain, fog, or poor conditions, or when following a motorcycle or large vehicle
answers.feedback: Correct! Adverse conditions, motorcycles, and large vehicles all require increased following distance.

answers.text: Driving below the speed limit
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Lower speeds don't necessarily require more following distance.

answers.text: Following another car of the same size
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Vehicle size doesn't determine following distance in normal conditions.

questions.text: When approaching a railroad crossing with flashing lights, you must:

answers.text: Stop at least 15 feet from the nearest rail and wait until it's safe to cross
answers.feedback: Correct! You must stop 15-50 feet from the tracks and wait for the lights to stop flashing.

answers.text: Slow down and cross quickly
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You must stop completely when lights are flashing.

answers.text: Only stop if you see a train approaching
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Flashing lights require you to stop immediately.

answers.text: Proceed if no train is visible
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Trains can arrive quickly - always stop for flashing lights.

questions.text: Pedestrians must be yielded the right-of-way:

answers.text: Only at marked crosswalks with signals
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Pedestrians have broader rights.

answers.text: At all marked and unmarked crosswalks
answers.feedback: Correct! Under F.S. 316.130 a driver must yield the right-of-way to a pedestrian in a crosswalk, marked or unmarked.

answers.text: Only when the walk signal is displayed
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Right-of-way extends beyond signalized crossings.

answers.text: Never - pedestrians must always yield to cars
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Pedestrians are vulnerable road users with right-of-way.

questions.text: Why is it important to give motorcyclists extra following distance?

answers.text: They are slower than cars
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Motorcycles often accelerate faster than cars.

answers.text: They can stop more quickly than cars and are harder to see
answers.feedback: Correct! Motorcycles can brake faster, and giving them space prevents rear-ending them.

answers.text: They are required to drive in the center of the lane
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Motorcycles can use any part of the lane.

answers.text: They must yield to all cars
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Motorcycles have the same rights as other vehicles.

questions.text: Commentary driving is a technique where you:

answers.text: Talk to passengers about road conditions
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This is a solo practice technique.

answers.text: Verbally describe what you see, predict, and plan while driving to stay mentally engaged
answers.feedback: Correct! Commentary driving keeps you alert and practices the IPDE process.

answers.text: Listen to radio commentary while driving
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This involves you actively narrating your observations.

answers.text: Write notes about your driving after each trip
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Commentary driving happens in real-time.

questions.text: Fines for speeding in a construction zone where workers are present are:

answers.text: The same as regular speeding fines
answers.feedback: Incorrect. With workers present, the construction-zone speeding fine is double the regular amount (F.S. 318.18(3)(e)).

answers.text: Doubled
answers.feedback: Correct. With construction personnel present or operating equipment, in a zone posted with the speed limit and notice that fines are doubled, the speeding fine is double the regular amount (F.S. 318.18(3)(e)).

answers.text: Tripled
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The fine is doubled, not tripled (F.S. 318.18(3)(e)).

answers.text: Waived if no workers are present
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Nothing is waived: with no workers present the regular fine applies, and the posted work-zone speed limit is still enforceable (F.S. 316.183(6)).

questions.text: In Florida, street racing can result in:

answers.text: A warning for first-time offenders
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Street racing carries serious penalties.

answers.text: License revocation for one year, vehicle impoundment, fines up to $5,000, and possible jail time
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida has strict penalties for street racing due to its extreme danger.

answers.text: Only a small fine
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Penalties are severe.

answers.text: Points on license but no other penalties
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Street racing results in license suspension and more.

questions.text: SCENARIO: You are approaching a green light at an intersection. As you enter, you notice a car approaching quickly from your left on the cross street. What IPDE step should you prioritize? Scenario Diagram:

answers.text: Identify - You correctly identified the potential hazard
answers.feedback: You already identified. Now you must predict and decide.

answers.text: Predict - Assume the other car might run the red light; prepare to brake
answers.feedback: Correct! Even with a green light, you must predict that others might not stop and be ready to execute defensive action.

answers.text: Decide - Decide to speed up to get through faster
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Speeding up increases risk in this situation.

answers.text: Execute - Maintain speed since you must be yielded the right-of-way
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Being yielded the right-of-way doesn't guarantee safety.

questions.text: SCENARIO: You are driving on a multi-lane highway. A large semi-truck is in the right lane ahead of you, and you want to merge right to take an upcoming exit. Where is the LEAST safe position relative to the truck?

answers.text: Directly beside the truck in the left lane
answers.feedback: This is also in the No-Zone but not the worst position.

answers.text: Directly behind the truck within 30 feet
answers.feedback: Correct! Directly behind a truck is the largest No-Zone - if the truck brakes suddenly, you can't see ahead and have no escape route.

answers.text: Well ahead of the truck in the right lane
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Being ahead with distance is safe.

answers.text: Two lanes to the left of the truck
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This provides adequate space.

questions.text: SCENARIO: You are driving on a narrow two-lane road (one lane each direction) at 30 MPH. A cyclist is ahead in your lane, riding about 2 feet from the curb. There is oncoming traffic, preventing you from moving into the opposite lane. What is the safest action?

answers.text: Pass the cyclist anyway, giving as much room as possible
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You cannot legally pass without 3 feet clearance.

answers.text: Slow down to match the cyclist's speed and wait for a safe opportunity to pass with 3+ feet clearance
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida law requires 3 feet. You must wait for safe passing conditions even if it means slowing significantly.

answers.text: Honk continuously until the cyclist moves over
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Cyclists have the right to use the full lane.

answers.text: Flash your lights to pressure the cyclist to speed up
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This is aggressive and unsafe.

questions.text: SCENARIO: You are driving on a highway with a posted speed limit of 65 MPH. It begins to rain heavily, reducing visibility to about 200 feet. Traffic is moving at 65 MPH. What should you do according to the Basic Speed Law?

answers.text: Continue at 65 MPH since that is the posted limit
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The Basic Speed Law requires adjusting for conditions.

answers.text: Reduce speed to 55 MPH or lower depending on conditions, even though the limit is 65 MPH
answers.feedback: Correct! The Basic Speed Law requires driving at a safe speed for conditions, which may be below the posted limit.

answers.text: Speed up to 70 MPH to get through the rain faster
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This violates the Basic Speed Law and increases risk.

answers.text: Pull over and stop on the highway shoulder
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Unless visibility is near zero, slowing down is safer than stopping on the shoulder.

questions.text: Which Smith System key is being applied when you maintain space around your vehicle and avoid being boxed in by other traffic?

answers.text: Aim High in Steering
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Aim High refers to looking ahead.

answers.text: Get the Big Picture
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Big Picture means scanning all around.

answers.text: Keep Your Eyes Moving
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This refers to continuous scanning.

answers.text: Leave Yourself an Out
answers.feedback: Correct! Leaving an out means always having an escape route in case of emergencies.

questions.text: According to the course, what is the leading cause of death for teenagers in the United States?

answers.text: Drug overdoses
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Motor vehicle crashes are the leading cause.

answers.text: Motor vehicle crashes
answers.feedback: Correct! Car crashes are the #1 killer of teens, which is why driver education is so critical.

answers.text: Violence
answers.feedback: Incorrect. While serious, crashes kill more teens.

answers.text: Sports injuries
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Traffic crashes far exceed sports-related deaths.

questions.text: Why is driving considered a privilege, not a right?

answers.text: Because it can be suspended or revoked if you violate traffic laws or demonstrate unsafe behavior
answers.feedback: Correct! Driving is a privilege granted by the state that comes with responsibilities and can be taken away.

answers.text: Because only wealthy people can afford cars
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Economic factors don't determine privilege vs. right.

answers.text: Because you must pay for a license
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The fee is not what makes it a privilege.

answers.text: Because driving is easy to learn
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Difficulty doesn't determine privilege status.

questions.text: The Smith System key "Make Sure They See You" is best applied by:

answers.text: Honking at every intersection
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Excessive honking is not appropriate.

answers.text: Using signals early, making eye contact, positioning your vehicle predictably, and using headlights
answers.feedback: Correct! Communication through signals, positioning, and visibility helps other drivers predict your actions.

answers.text: Driving faster than traffic
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Speed doesn't equal visibility or predictability.

answers.text: Using high beams at all times
answers.feedback: Incorrect. High beams blind other drivers in many situations.

questions.text: Total stopping distance consists of:

answers.text: Only braking distance
answers.feedback: Incorrect. There are two components.

answers.text: Reaction distance plus braking distance
answers.feedback: Correct! Total stopping distance includes the distance traveled during reaction time PLUS the distance to stop after braking.

answers.text: Only reaction distance
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You must also account for braking distance.

answers.text: Reaction distance, braking distance, plus thinking distance
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Thinking is part of reaction time, not separate.

questions.text: When managing your space cushion, you should:

answers.text: Only worry about the space in front of your vehicle
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You need space all around.

answers.text: Create and maintain space on all sides of your vehicle - front, rear, and sides
answers.feedback: Correct! A proper space cushion means managing space in all directions, giving you escape routes.

answers.text: Stay close to other vehicles to maintain traffic flow
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This eliminates your safety cushion.

answers.text: Only maintain space on your left side
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You need space all around your vehicle.

quizzes.title: Lesson 2.1 Knowledge Check: Traffic Signs

questions.text: Which shape is used exclusively for stop signs?

answers.text: Triangle
answers.feedback: Incorrect. An inverted triangle is used for yield signs. The octagon (8-sided shape) is the shape used exclusively for stop signs.

answers.text: Diamond
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Diamonds are used for warning signs. The octagon (8-sided shape) is used exclusively for stop signs.

answers.text: Octagon
answers.feedback: Correct! The octagon (8-sided shape) is used only for stop signs. This unique shape allows drivers to recognize it from any direction, even from the back.

answers.text: Pentagon
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Pentagons are used for school zone signs. The octagon (8-sided shape) is used exclusively for stop signs.

questions.text: On U.S. highways, blue signs indicate:

answers.text: Construction zones
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Orange signs indicate construction zones. Blue signs point to motorist services like gas, food, lodging, and hospitals.

answers.text: Motorist services (gas, food, lodging, hospitals)
answers.feedback: Correct! Blue highway signs direct you to motorist services — gas stations, restaurants, hotels, and hospitals near upcoming exits.

answers.text: Recreational areas and parks
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Brown signs indicate recreational areas and parks. Blue signs point to motorist services like gas, food, lodging, and hospitals.

answers.text: Speed regulations
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Speed regulations use white regulatory signs. Blue signs indicate motorist services like gas, food, lodging, and hospitals.

questions.text: A yellow diamond-shaped sign typically indicates:

answers.text: A law you must obey
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Regulatory signs (usually white rectangles) tell you about laws. Yellow diamonds are warning signs that alert you to hazards or road changes ahead.

answers.text: A warning about a potential hazard ahead
answers.feedback: Correct! Yellow diamond signs are warning signs. They alert you to hazards or changes ahead — curves, intersections, pedestrian crossings, and more — so you can prepare.

answers.text: Navigation directions to a destination
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Green rectangular signs provide navigation directions. Yellow diamonds are warning signs that alert you to hazards or changes in the road ahead.

answers.text: A school zone boundary
answers.feedback: Incorrect. School zone signs are fluorescent yellow-green pentagons. Yellow diamond signs are general warning signs for hazards and road changes ahead.

questions.text: A pennant-shaped (triangular) sign placed on the left side of the road indicates:

answers.text: Yield ahead
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Yield signs are inverted triangles. The pennant shape (placed on the left side of the road) marks a no-passing zone.

answers.text: No passing zone
answers.feedback: Correct! The pennant shape is used exclusively to mark no-passing zones. It's placed on the left side of the road to face drivers who might attempt to pass.

answers.text: Merge left
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Merge signs are yellow diamonds. The pennant shape placed on the left side of the road means no passing zone.

answers.text: School crossing
answers.feedback: Incorrect. School crossings use pentagon-shaped signs. The pennant shape on the left side of the road indicates a no-passing zone.

questions.text: A circular yellow sign with the letters "RR" warns you of:

answers.text: A rest area ahead
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Rest areas are shown on blue or green guide signs. The circular yellow "RR" sign is the advance warning for a railroad crossing ahead.

answers.text: A roundabout ahead
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Roundabouts use a diamond-shaped warning sign with circular arrows. The circular yellow "RR" sign warns of a railroad crossing ahead.

answers.text: A railroad crossing ahead
answers.feedback: Correct! The circular yellow sign with "RR" is the advance warning for a railroad crossing. It's the only circular warning sign, making it uniquely identifiable.

answers.text: A road repair zone
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Road repair zones use orange construction signs. The circular yellow "RR" sign is the advance warning for a railroad crossing ahead.

quizzes.title: Lesson 2.2 Knowledge Check: Traffic Signals and Pavement Markings

questions.text: A steady yellow traffic light means:

answers.text: Speed up to clear the intersection before it turns red
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Speeding up to "beat the light" is dangerous and a leading cause of intersection crashes. A steady yellow means prepare to stop if you safely can.

answers.text: The light is about to turn red — stop if you can do so safely
answers.feedback: Correct! A steady yellow means the light is about to turn red. If you can stop safely before the intersection, you must stop. If you're too close to stop safely, proceed with caution.

answers.text: Proceed with caution but do not stop
answers.feedback: Incorrect. That describes a flashing yellow, not a steady yellow. A steady yellow means the light is about to turn red — stop if you can do so safely.

answers.text: Yield to cross traffic only
answers.feedback: Incorrect. A steady yellow light means the signal is about to turn red. If you can stop safely, you must do so — not just yield.

questions.text: A green arrow signal means:

answers.text: Yield to oncoming traffic, then turn
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Yielding to oncoming traffic describes a flashing yellow arrow (unprotected turn). A green arrow gives you a protected turn — oncoming traffic is stopped.

answers.text: You have a protected turn — oncoming traffic is stopped
answers.feedback: Correct! A green arrow means you have a protected turn. Oncoming traffic has a red light, so you can turn without yielding — but always watch for pedestrians in the crosswalk.

answers.text: Turn only if no pedestrians are visible
answers.feedback: Incorrect. While you should always watch for pedestrians, a green arrow specifically means you have a protected turn — oncoming traffic has a red light.

answers.text: The turn lane is closing — merge out
answers.feedback: Incorrect. A green arrow indicates a protected turn, meaning oncoming traffic is stopped for you. It has nothing to do with lane closures.

questions.text: Double solid yellow lines on the road indicate:

answers.text: Passing is allowed when safe
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Passing is allowed with broken (dashed) yellow lines. Double solid yellow lines prohibit passing in both directions.

answers.text: No passing in either direction
answers.feedback: Correct! Double solid yellow lines mean no passing in either direction. You may cross them only to turn into a driveway or side road — never to pass another vehicle.

answers.text: Lane changes are permitted
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Yellow lines separate opposing traffic, not same-direction lanes. Double solid yellow lines mean no passing in either direction.

answers.text: The road is one-way
answers.feedback: Incorrect. One-way roads typically use white lines. Yellow lines separate traffic going in opposite directions. Double solid yellow lines mean no passing allowed.

questions.text: A flashing red traffic signal should be treated as:

answers.text: A yield sign
answers.feedback: Incorrect. A flashing yellow light is like a yield (proceed with caution). A flashing red light must be treated as a stop sign — full stop required.

answers.text: A stop sign
answers.feedback: Correct! A flashing red light is treated exactly like a stop sign. Come to a complete stop, check for traffic and pedestrians, and proceed when safe.

answers.text: A broken traffic light — proceed normally
answers.feedback: Incorrect. A flashing red is a deliberate signal, not a malfunction. Treat it as a stop sign: stop completely, then proceed when safe.

answers.text: A green light with caution
answers.feedback: Incorrect. A flashing red is not a green light — it requires a complete stop, just like a stop sign. Check for traffic, then proceed when safe.

questions.text: In Florida, which statement about turning on red is correct?

answers.text: You may turn right on a steady red after a complete stop, unless a sign prohibits it
answers.feedback: Correct! In Florida, you may turn right on a steady red circular signal after coming to a complete stop, unless a "No Turn on Red" sign is posted. You may NOT turn on a red arrow.

answers.text: You may turn right on a red arrow after a complete stop
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You cannot turn on a red arrow in Florida. A red arrow means no turning in that direction — period. Right on red is only allowed on a steady red circular signal after a complete stop.

answers.text: You may turn left on red from a one-way onto a one-way without stopping
answers.feedback: Incorrect. While left on red from a one-way to a one-way may be allowed after a complete stop, this answer says "without stopping," which is never correct. The correct answer is right on red after a complete stop unless a sign prohibits it.

answers.text: Right on red is never allowed in Florida
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Right on red IS allowed in Florida — after a complete stop, unless a "No Turn on Red" sign is posted. It's a standard rule across most U.S. states.

quizzes.title: Lesson 2.3 Knowledge Check: Construction and School Zones

questions.text: Construction zone signs are identified by what color?

answers.text: Yellow
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Yellow is used for general warning signs. Construction zones use orange signs and devices.

answers.text: Orange
answers.feedback: Correct! Orange is the designated color for all construction and work zone signs and devices. When you see orange, increase your attention and reduce speed.

answers.text: Red
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Red is used for stop, yield, and prohibition. Construction zone signs are orange.

answers.text: Fluorescent green
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Fluorescent yellow-green is used for school zones and pedestrian crossings. Construction zones use orange.

questions.text: A flagger in a construction zone holds up a STOP paddle. You must:

answers.text: Slow down and proceed with caution
answers.feedback: Incorrect. That's the response for a SLOW paddle. A STOP paddle requires a complete stop — wait for the flagger to direct you forward.

answers.text: Stop completely and wait for the flagger to signal you to proceed
answers.feedback: Correct! A flagger's instructions override all other signals. When they hold up STOP, come to a complete stop and wait for their signal to proceed.

answers.text: Use your own judgment about whether it's safe to proceed
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Flagger instructions override your own judgment. There may be hazards you cannot see. Always obey the flagger.

answers.text: Stop only if workers are directly in your path
answers.feedback: Incorrect. A STOP paddle means stop completely, regardless of where workers are. The flagger has information about conditions you may not be able to see.

questions.text: In most Florida school zones, the speed limit when the zone is active is:

answers.feedback: Incorrect. 25–30 mph is too fast for a school zone. Florida school zones typically require 15–20 mph when the zone is active.
Correct! Most Florida school zones have speed limits of 15–20 mph when active. Always check the posted sign for the exact speed in each zone.

answers.text: 10 mph
answers.feedback: Incorrect. While 10 mph would be very cautious, the standard Florida school zone speed limit is 15–20 mph. Check the posted sign for the exact limit.

answers.text: 35 mph
answers.feedback: Incorrect. 35 mph is far too fast for a school zone. Florida school zones typically require 15–20 mph when children may be present.

questions.text: In Florida, when must you stop for a school bus with its red lights flashing?

answers.text: Only if you're behind the bus
answers.feedback: Incorrect. In Florida, traffic in BOTH directions must stop — not just vehicles behind the bus. The only exception is a raised median separating the lanes.

answers.text: In both directions, unless separated by a raised median
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida law requires traffic from both directions to stop for a school bus with red lights flashing. The only exception is if a raised median or physical barrier separates you from the bus.

answers.text: Only during school hours
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You must stop for a school bus with flashing red lights at any time, not just during school hours. Children may ride buses for field trips and other activities.

answers.text: Never — school buses have their own rules
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Passing a stopped school bus with red lights flashing is a serious traffic violation in Florida, with a minimum penalty of $265 ($200 civil penalty plus a $65 surcharge).

questions.text: In Florida, traffic fines are doubled in which of the following zones?

answers.text: Hospital zones only
answers.feedback: Incorrect. While you should drive carefully near hospitals, doubled fines specifically apply to active construction zones and school zones in Florida.

answers.text: Highway rest areas
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Rest areas don't have doubled fines. Florida doubles fines in active construction zones and school zones to protect workers and children.

answers.text: Active construction zones and school zones
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida law doubles traffic fines in active construction zones and school zones. This applies to speeding, reckless driving, and other moving violations.

answers.text: Residential neighborhoods
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Residential neighborhoods don't have doubled fines by default. The doubled-fine law applies specifically to construction zones and school zones.

quizzes.title: Lesson 2.4 Knowledge Check: Right-of-Way Rules

questions.text: At an all-way stop, two vehicles arrive at the same time. Which vehicle is yielded the right-of-way?

answers.text: The vehicle on the left
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The vehicle on the LEFT must yield. When arriving at the same time, the vehicle to the RIGHT is yielded the right-of-way.

answers.text: The vehicle on the right
answers.feedback: Correct! When two vehicles arrive at an all-way stop simultaneously, the vehicle to the right must be yielded the right-of-way.

answers.text: The larger vehicle
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Vehicle size doesn't determine right-of-way. The vehicle to the right is yielded the right-of-way when two vehicles arrive simultaneously.

answers.text: The vehicle that honks first
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Honking doesn't determine right-of-way. The vehicle to the right is yielded the right-of-way when two arrive at the same time.

questions.text: When entering a roundabout, you must yield to:

answers.text: Vehicles approaching the roundabout from the left
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You yield to vehicles already inside the roundabout, not just those approaching from a specific direction.

answers.text: Vehicles already circling inside the roundabout
answers.feedback: Correct! Vehicles already inside the roundabout must be yielded the right-of-way. Wait at the yield sign for a safe gap before entering.

answers.text: No one — it's first-come, first-served
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Roundabouts are not first-come-first-served. Vehicles already circling inside always must be yielded the right-of-way.

answers.text: Only pedestrians, not other vehicles
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You must yield to both pedestrians AND vehicles already in the roundabout. You must yield to traffic inside the circle.

questions.text: When an emergency vehicle with activated lights and sirens approaches from behind, you should:

answers.text: Speed up to get out of the way
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Speeding up is dangerous. Pull over to the closest edge of the roadway, clear of any intersection, and stop to give the emergency vehicle a clear path.

answers.text: Stop immediately wherever you are
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Don't stop in the middle of the road — you could block the emergency vehicle. Pull over to the closest edge of the roadway first, clear of any intersection, then stop.

answers.text: Pull over to the closest edge of the roadway, clear of any intersection, and stop
answers.feedback: Correct! Pull over to the closest edge of the roadway, clear of any intersection, and stop. Stay stopped until the emergency vehicle has passed. If you are in an intersection, clear it first, then pull over.

answers.text: Move to the left lane
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Move to the closest edge of the roadway — on an ordinary two-way street that is the right-hand edge. Emergency vehicles need a clear path, so clear the lane and stop.

questions.text: In Florida, pedestrians must be yielded the right-of-way in a crosswalk:

answers.text: Only at marked crosswalks with painted lines
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Pedestrians must be yielded the right-of-way at BOTH marked and unmarked crosswalks. Unmarked crosswalks exist at every intersection with sidewalks.

answers.text: Only when the pedestrian signal shows "Walk"
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Drivers must yield to pedestrians in crosswalks regardless of what the pedestrian signal shows. Pedestrians must be yielded the right-of-way at both marked and unmarked crosswalks.

answers.text: At both marked and unmarked crosswalks
answers.feedback: Correct! Pedestrians must be yielded the right-of-way at both marked and unmarked crosswalks. An unmarked crosswalk exists at any intersection where sidewalks are present.

answers.text: Only during daylight hours
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Pedestrian right-of-way applies at all hours, day or night. Drivers must yield at both marked and unmarked crosswalks.

questions.text: Florida's "Move Over" law requires you to do what when passing a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights on the shoulder?

answers.text: Honk to warn the officer
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Honking is unnecessary and unhelpful. The law requires you to move over one lane or slow to 20 mph below the posted speed limit.

answers.text: Move over one lane or slow to 20 mph below the speed limit
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida's Move Over law requires you to move over one full lane when possible, or slow to 20 mph below the speed limit. This applies to stopped emergency, sanitation, utility service, wrecker, and road and bridge maintenance or construction vehicles — and, since January 1, 2024, to any disabled vehicle displaying hazard lights, flares or emergency signage, or with people visibly present (F.S. 316.126(1)(b)).

answers.text: Stop completely and wait
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You don't need to stop completely. Move over one lane if possible, or slow to 20 mph below the speed limit.

answers.text: Speed up to pass quickly
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Speeding up is dangerous and illegal near stopped emergency vehicles. Move over or slow down significantly.

quizzes.title: Lesson 2.5 Knowledge Check: Complex Intersections and Turning

questions.text: When making an unprotected left turn at a solid green light, you must:

answers.text: Turn immediately — green means go
