answers.feedback: Incorrect. A solid green doesn't mean "turn immediately." Oncoming traffic also has green. You must yield to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians first.

answers.text: Yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians before turning
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You don't need a green arrow — you can turn on a solid green, but you must yield to oncoming traffic. A green arrow would make it protected.

answers.text: Wait for a green arrow before turning
Honk to warn oncoming traffic you're turning
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Honking is not a substitute for yielding. You must wait for a safe gap in oncoming traffic before making the turn.

questions.text: When making a left turn from the inner (leftmost) turn lane, you should turn into:

answers.text: Any available lane on the cross street
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You must stay in your lane throughout the turn. Inner lane turns into the innermost lane — changing lanes during a turn is dangerous.

answers.text: The rightmost lane of the cross street
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Turning into the rightmost lane from the inner turn lane would cut across other turning traffic. Turn into the innermost (leftmost) lane.

answers.text: The innermost (leftmost) lane of the cross street
answers.feedback: Correct! In a multi-lane turn, finish in the same lane you started. Inner turn lane → innermost lane of the cross street.

answers.text: The center lane of the cross street
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The center lane would be correct only if you're in the outer turn lane. From the inner turn lane, go to the innermost (leftmost) lane.

questions.text: In Florida, right turn on red is prohibited when:

answers.text: It's nighttime
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Time of day doesn't affect right-on-red rules. It's prohibited by "No Turn on Red" signs or red arrows.

answers.text: A "No Turn on Red" sign is posted or a red arrow is displayed
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The number of lanes doesn't determine right-on-red rules. Look for "No Turn on Red" signs and red arrows.

answers.text: There are more than two lanes on the cross street
You're the first car at the intersection
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Your position in line doesn't matter. Right on red is prohibited by "No Turn on Red" signs or red arrows.

questions.text: Florida law requires you to signal before turning for at least the last:

answers.text: 50 feet
answers.feedback: Incorrect. 50 feet is too short. Florida requires signaling for at least 100 feet before a turn.

answers.text: 100 feet
answers.feedback: Incorrect. While signaling early is good practice, the legal minimum in Florida is 100 feet, not 200.

answers.text: 200 feet
Only when other cars are nearby
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You must signal regardless of whether other cars are visible. The law requires 100 feet of signal before turning.

questions.text: While waiting to make a left turn, your front wheels should be pointed:

answers.text: To the left, ready for the turn
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Never point wheels left while waiting. If you're rear-ended, you'd be pushed into oncoming traffic. Keep them straight ahead.

answers.text: Straight ahead
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Wheels should point straight ahead, not to the right. This prevents being pushed into oncoming traffic if rear-ended.

answers.text: To the right
It doesn't matter
answers.feedback: Incorrect. It absolutely matters. Keep wheels straight to prevent being pushed into oncoming traffic if hit from behind.

quizzes.title: Lesson 2.6 Knowledge Check: Highway Driving and Lane Usage

questions.text: The purpose of an acceleration lane (on-ramp merge lane) is to:

answers.text: Give you a place to stop and wait for a gap
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Stopping at the end of an acceleration lane is extremely dangerous. Its purpose is to accelerate to highway speed, not to stop.

answers.text: Allow you to build speed to match highway traffic before merging
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The acceleration lane is for building speed to merge, not for slow-speed driving. You must match highway speed before entering traffic.

answers.text: Provide a slow lane for vehicles under the speed limit
Let you check your phone before entering the highway
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You should never use your phone while driving. The acceleration lane is for building speed to merge safely onto the highway.

questions.text: Florida's "Slower Traffic Keep Right" law means:

answers.text: You can drive in any lane at any speed
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Each lane has a purpose. The left lane is reserved for passing. Slower traffic must stay right.

answers.text: The left lane is for passing only — move right if not actively passing
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The shoulder is for emergencies, not for driving. Slower traffic should use the right lane, not the shoulder.

answers.text: Slow vehicles must use the shoulder
This law only applies to trucks
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The law applies to ALL vehicles, not just trucks. If you're not passing, move to the right lane.

questions.text: If you miss your highway exit, you should:

answers.text: Stop and back up on the shoulder
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Backing up on a highway is illegal and extremely dangerous. Continue to the next exit instead.

answers.text: Continue to the next exit and turn around
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Crossing the median is illegal and can cause head-on collisions. Proceed to the next exit.

answers.text: Cross the median to make a U-turn
Cut across the grass to reach the ramp
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Driving off the highway onto grass or through undesignated areas is dangerous and illegal. Take the next exit.

questions.text: Florida express lanes separated by double solid white lines and pylons can be entered:

answers.text: Anywhere along the lane
answers.feedback: Incorrect. You can only enter at designated openings. The double solid white lines and pylons are barriers — crossing them is illegal and dangerous.

answers.text: Only at designated openings marked with dashed lines
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Express lanes can be used during any hours they're open, but you must enter only at designated openings with dashed markings.

answers.text: Only during non-peak hours
By crossing the pylons carefully
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Crossing pylons is illegal and dangerous — they're barriers. Use only designated openings with dashed lines.

questions.text: When exiting a highway, you should begin slowing down:

answers.text: While still on the main highway
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Don't slow down on the main highway — that's unexpected for drivers behind you. Wait until you're in the deceleration lane/exit ramp.

answers.text: After entering the deceleration lane (exit ramp)
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Waiting until the curve is too late — you need to begin slowing as soon as you enter the deceleration lane, well before the curve.

answers.text: Only after you see the ramp curve ahead
In the center lane before moving right
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Don't slow in the center lane. Move to the right lane first, then enter the deceleration lane before braking.

quizzes.title: Lesson 2.7 Knowledge Check — Railroad Crossings

questions.text: Under Florida law (F.S. § 316.159), how far must you stop from the nearest rail at a railroad crossing with active signals?

answers.text: Within 5 feet of the crossing gate
At least 15 feet, but no more than 50 feet, from the nearest rail
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida law requires you to stop at least 15 feet (and no more than 50 feet) from the nearest rail when signals are active. This keeps you clear of the train while still close enough to see the signals.

answers.text: At least 100 feet from the nearest rail
Anywhere on the road before the tracks is fine, as long as you're not on the tracks

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida law (F.S. § 316.159) requires stopping at least 15 feet — but no more than 50 feet — from the nearest rail at an active crossing. Closer than 15 ft puts you in the path of a passing train; further than 50 ft and you may not see when the signals clear.

questions.text: After a train passes at a crossing with multiple tracks, you should:

answers.text: Cross immediately — the train has cleared the area.
Wait for the gate to fully raise, then check for a second train on adjacent tracks before proceeding.
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. The 'second train trap' — a second train coming on the adjacent track from the opposite direction, hidden by the first train's noise — is a leading cause of fatal crossing crashes. Always wait for the full all-clear and check both ways before moving.

answers.text: Honk before crossing to alert any other trains.
Drive around the gate as soon as the visible train has passed.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. After one train passes a multi-track crossing, a second train may be approaching on the adjacent track — its noise hidden by the first train. Wait for the gate to fully raise and the lights to stop flashing, then check both directions before moving.

questions.text: If your vehicle stalls on railroad tracks, what is the safest first action?

answers.text: Try to restart the engine first.
Stay in the car and hope the train can stop in time.
Get everyone out immediately and move away from the tracks at a 45° angle in the direction the train is coming from.
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. The vehicle is replaceable; you are not. Get out immediately and move at a 45° angle toward the train's approach direction — the train will push debris in its direction of travel, so the angle keeps you out of the wreckage path.

answers.text: Try to push the car off the tracks.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. If you stall on the tracks, get everyone out immediately. Move at a 45° angle TOWARD the train's approach direction — debris is pushed in the train's direction of travel, so this angle keeps you safe. Never try to restart or push the car. A freight train at 55 mph needs over a mile to stop.

questions.text: Which of the following vehicles must stop at ALL railroad crossings, even crossings without active signals?

answers.text: Motorcycles and mopeds
Pickup trucks and SUVs
Vehicles with more than four passengers
School buses and vehicles carrying hazardous materials
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. Florida Statute § 316.159 requires school buses (with or without students aboard) and vehicles carrying placarded hazardous materials to stop at every railroad crossing — even passive crossings. Never pass these vehicles when they're stopped at a crossing.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida law requires school buses and hazmat-carrying vehicles to stop at every railroad crossing — including passive crossings with just a crossbuck. Standard passenger vehicles, motorcycles, and SUVs do not have this requirement. If you're behind one of these vehicles, expect the stop and never pass them.

questions.text: A lowered railroad crossing gate means:

answers.text: It is illegal to drive around it under any circumstances — you must wait.
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. Driving around a lowered gate is illegal in Florida (and every other state) and frequently fatal. The gate is down because the signal system detected a train — even if you can't see one yet. Wait for the lights to stop and the gate to fully raise.

answers.text: You may drive around it if you can clearly see no train is coming.
You may drive around it after looking both ways.
You may proceed cautiously if the gate has been down for more than 30 seconds.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. A lowered gate is non-negotiable. It is illegal to drive around one in Florida — and the most common cause of fatal crossing crashes is exactly this. Even if you 'can see no train is coming,' the signal system has detected one. Always wait for the full all-clear: lights off, gate fully raised.

quizzes.title: Lesson 2.8 Knowledge Check — Law Enforcement & The Move Over Law

questions.text: Under Florida's Move Over Law (F.S. § 316.126), what must you do when approaching a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights on a multi-lane road?

answers.text: Maintain your speed if the vehicle is on the shoulder.
Move over one lane away if it is safe to do so; if not, slow to 20 mph below the posted speed limit.
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida's Move Over Law requires you to move over one lane when approaching an emergency, law enforcement, utility, tow, sanitation, or disabled vehicle displaying flashers. If you cannot safely move over, slow to 20 mph below the posted limit. The 5 mph alternative applies only on roads with a posted limit of 20 mph or less.

answers.text: Always come to a complete stop on the shoulder behind the emergency vehicle.
Slow to 5 mph regardless of the posted speed limit.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida Move Over Law: move over one lane if safe, otherwise slow to 20 mph below the posted limit. Maintaining speed or stopping behind the vehicle are both wrong — the law is specifically designed to give the roadside worker a buffer of distance or a major reduction in approach speed.

questions.text: If the posted speed limit is 20 mph or less, the Move Over Law requires you to slow to what speed when you cannot move over?

answers.text: 0 mph (full stop)
5 mph
answers.feedback: Correct! When the posted speed limit is 20 mph or less, Florida law requires slowing to 5 mph. The standard '20 mph below the posted limit' rule doesn't work at low speeds, so the statute specifies 5 mph as the floor.

answers.text: 10 mph
The posted speed limit (no reduction needed)

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. On roads with a posted limit of 20 mph or less, Florida specifies 5 mph as the slow-down minimum when you can't move over. The '20 mph below the limit' rule would result in negative or zero speed at low posted limits, so 5 mph is the statutory minimum.

questions.text: When you are stopped by law enforcement at night, which action is recommended to show the officer you are not a threat?

answers.text: Step out of the vehicle immediately to meet the officer.
Turn on your interior dome light and keep both hands visible on the steering wheel.
answers.feedback: Correct! At night, turning on your interior dome light dramatically improves the officer's ability to see you and assess the situation safely. Keep your hands visibly on the wheel and wait — do not reach for documents until asked. Both of these signal that you have nothing to hide and have no sudden, unexpected movements.

answers.text: Reach into the glove box to get your registration before the officer arrives.
Roll down all four windows and put your hands out the driver's window.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Stepping out is dangerous and looks confrontational. Reaching for the glove box before being asked is the most common reason traffic stops escalate — the officer can't see what you're grabbing. The right call at night is: dome light on, window down, hands on the wheel, wait for instructions.

questions.text: You arrive at an intersection where the traffic signal is completely dark and no officer is present. How should you treat it?

answers.text: As a yield sign — slow down and proceed if no one is coming.
Continue through at normal speed if no other cars are visible.
As an all-way stop — every direction stops, then proceeds in arrival order.
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida law treats a completely dark or out-of-service traffic signal as an all-way stop. Every direction stops, then proceeds in arrival order. If two arrive at the same time, the driver on the right must be yielded the right-of-way. If you arrive opposite each other simultaneously, the driver turning left must yield to the driver going straight or turning right.

answers.text: As a flashing yellow light — proceed with caution.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. A dark traffic signal isn't 'no signal' — it's an all-way stop under Florida law. Every direction stops first, then proceeds in order of arrival. Treating it as a yield, flashing yellow, or open intersection puts you and others at risk because not every driver will make the same assumption.

questions.text: A law enforcement officer is directing traffic at an intersection where the signal shows green in your direction. What should you do?

answers.text: Continue through — your light is green.
Honk to alert the officer that your light is green.
Follow the officer's directions — they override the traffic signal.
answers.feedback: Correct! Under Florida F.S. § 316.072, you follow the officer, not the signal: F.S. § 316.072(3) makes it unlawful — a second-degree misdemeanor — willfully to fail or refuse to comply with an officer's lawful order or direction. If the officer has their palm out toward you, you stop — even on green. If they beckon you forward, you go — even on red. Disobeying an officer's traffic-direction signal is a moving violation and can result in obstruction charges if it endangers the officer.

answers.text: Stop in the intersection and wait for the officer to clear out.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. An officer directing traffic always overrides the signal. Continuing through a green light when the officer is signaling you to stop is a violation under Florida F.S. § 316.072. Honking and stopping in the intersection both create danger. Watch the officer's hand: palm out = stop; beckoning = proceed; pointing = turn that direction.

quizzes.title: Unit 2 Summative Assessment: The Language of the Road

questions.text: A diamond-shaped sign with a yellow background indicates:

answers.text: A regulatory law you must obey
A warning about a hazard or road change ahead
answers.feedback: Correct! Yellow diamond signs are warning signs alerting you to hazards or changes ahead. (Lesson 2.1)

answers.text: A guide to a nearby destination
A construction zone ahead

questions.text: Which sign shape is used only for stop signs?

answers.text: Circle
Pentagon
Octagon
answers.feedback: Correct! The octagon (8 sides) is used exclusively for stop signs. (Lesson 2.1)

answers.text: Diamond

questions.text: Brown highway signs indicate:

answers.text: Motorist services
Recreational areas and cultural points of interest
answers.feedback: Correct! Brown signs point to parks, recreation areas, and cultural landmarks. Blue = services, orange = construction. (Lesson 2.1)

answers.text: Construction zones
Speed regulations

questions.text: A pennant-shaped sign on the left side of the road means:

answers.text: School zone ahead
No passing zone
answers.feedback: Correct! The pennant shape is used exclusively for no-passing zones, placed on the left side of the road. (Lesson 2.1)

answers.text: Merge ahead
Railroad crossing

questions.text: A flashing red traffic light should be treated as:

answers.text: A yield sign
A green light with caution
A stop sign
answers.feedback: Correct! A flashing red = stop sign. Stop completely, check traffic, proceed when safe. (Lesson 2.2)

answers.text: A broken signal — proceed normally

questions.text: A green arrow signal gives you a:

answers.text: Protected turn — oncoming traffic is stopped
answers.feedback: Correct! A green arrow = protected turn. Oncoming traffic has a red light. Still check for pedestrians. (Lesson 2.2)

answers.text: Unprotected turn — yield to oncoming traffic
Permission to turn only if no pedestrians are visible
Suggestion to turn, but it's optional

questions.text: Yellow center lines separate traffic moving in:

answers.text: The same direction
Opposite directions
answers.feedback: Correct! Yellow lines separate opposing traffic. White lines separate same-direction traffic. (Lesson 2.2)

answers.text: Toward an exit ramp
Into a bike lane

questions.text: In Florida, you may NOT turn on a:

answers.text: Steady red circular signal (after stopping)
Flashing yellow arrow
Red arrow signal
answers.feedback: Correct! A red arrow prohibits all turning in that direction. Unlike a steady red circle, you cannot turn on a red arrow even after stopping. (Lesson 2.2)

answers.text: Steady green circular signal

questions.text: Construction zone signs are identified by which color?

answers.text: Yellow
Red
Orange
answers.feedback: Correct! Orange = construction/work zones. Yellow = general warnings. (Lesson 2.3)

answers.text: Green

questions.text: In Florida, traffic fines in active construction and school zones are:

answers.text: The same as regular fines
Doubled
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida doubles fines in active construction and school zones. (Lesson 2.3)

answers.text: Tripled
Waived if no workers are present

questions.text: Florida school zones typically have a speed limit of:

answers.feedback: Correct! Most Florida school zones are 15-20 mph when active. (Lesson 2.3)

answers.text: 35 mph
10 mph

questions.text: When a school bus activates its red flashing lights and stop arm on a two-lane road, you must:

answers.text: Stop only if you're behind the bus
Slow down to 15 mph and proceed
Stop in both directions until the stop arm retracts
answers.feedback: Correct! Both directions must stop on a two-lane road. Exception only with a raised median. (Lesson 2.3)

answers.text: Stop only during school hours

questions.text: At an all-way stop, if two vehicles arrive at the same time, who is yielded the right-of-way?

answers.text: The vehicle on the left
The vehicle on the right
answers.feedback: Correct! Vehicle on the right is yielded the right-of-way when arriving simultaneously. (Lesson 2.4)

answers.text: The larger vehicle
Whoever signals first

questions.text: When entering a roundabout, you must yield to:

answers.text: No one — first come, first served
Vehicles already inside the roundabout
answers.feedback: Correct! Vehicles in the roundabout always must be yielded the right-of-way. Wait for a safe gap. (Lesson 2.4)

answers.text: Only pedestrians
Vehicles approaching from the right only

questions.text: When an emergency vehicle with lights and sirens approaches, you should:

answers.text: Speed up to clear the way
Pull over to the closest edge of the roadway, clear of any intersection, and stop
answers.feedback: Correct! Pull over to the closest edge of the roadway, clear of any intersection, and stop until the emergency vehicle passes. (Lesson 2.4)

answers.text: Move to the left lane
Stop immediately in your current lane

questions.text: Florida's "Move Over" law requires you to move over one lane or slow to ___ below the speed limit when passing a stopped emergency vehicle.

answers.text: 10 mph
20 mph
answers.feedback: Correct! Move over one lane, or slow to 20 mph below the posted speed limit. (Lesson 2.4)

answers.text: 30 mph
5 mph

questions.text: Pedestrians must be yielded the right-of-way at:

answers.text: Marked crosswalks only
Both marked and unmarked crosswalks
answers.feedback: Correct! Both marked AND unmarked crosswalks. Unmarked crosswalks exist at every intersection with sidewalks. (Lesson 2.4)

answers.text: Nowhere — pedestrians must always yield to vehicles
Only when a crossing guard is present

questions.text: An unprotected left turn on a solid green light requires you to:

answers.text: Turn immediately
Yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians before turning
answers.feedback: Correct! Unprotected = oncoming traffic has green too. Yield and wait for a safe gap. (Lesson 2.5)

answers.text: Wait for a green arrow
Turn your wheels left while waiting

questions.text: While waiting to make a left turn, your wheels should be pointed:

answers.text: Left, toward your intended turn
Right, for safety
Straight ahead
answers.feedback: Correct! Straight ahead. If rear-ended with wheels turned left, you'd be pushed into oncoming traffic. (Lesson 2.5)

answers.text: It doesn't matter

questions.text: Florida law requires you to activate your turn signal at least ___ before turning.

answers.text: 50 feet
100 feet
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida law requires continuous signaling for at least 100 feet before a turn (F.S. 316.155). (Lesson 2.5)

answers.text: 200 feet
Only when others are nearby

questions.text: In a multi-lane left turn, you should finish your turn in:

answers.text: Any lane you prefer
The same lane position you started in
answers.feedback: Correct! Stay in your lane throughout the turn. Inner lane → inner lane, outer → outer. Change lanes after completing the turn. (Lesson 2.5)

answers.text: The rightmost lane
The center lane always

questions.text: The purpose of an acceleration lane is to:

answers.text: Provide a stopping area before the highway
Build speed to match highway traffic before merging
answers.feedback: Correct! Use the acceleration lane to reach highway speed before merging. Never stop at the end. (Lesson 2.6)

answers.text: Allow slow vehicles to travel below the minimum speed
Give trucks a separate lane

questions.text: According to Florida law, the left lane on a highway is for:

answers.text: Driving at any speed
Passing only — move right when not passing
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida's Slower Traffic Keep Right law — left lane is for passing only. You can be cited for left-lane camping. (Lesson 2.6)

answers.text: The fastest vehicles only
Merging traffic

questions.text: If you miss your highway exit, you should:

answers.text: Back up on the shoulder
Cross the median
Continue to the next exit
answers.feedback: Correct! Continue to the next exit. Never stop, back up, or cross the median. A few extra minutes is better than a crash. (Lesson 2.6)

answers.text: Stop in the right lane

questions.text: When exiting a highway, you should begin slowing down:

answers.text: On the main highway before the exit
After entering the deceleration lane (exit ramp)
answers.feedback: Correct! Slow down in the deceleration lane/exit ramp, not on the main highway. Braking on the highway causes rear-end crashes. (Lesson 2.6)

answers.text: Only when you see the ramp curve
In the center lane

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.1: Knowledge Check — Vehicle Systems & Pre-Drive Checks

questions.text: A red warning light on your dashboard typically indicates:

answers.text: Everything is functioning normally.
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Red lights never mean normal operation — they indicate a serious problem. Green or blue lights indicate normal operation of systems like turn signals or high beams.

answers.text: A serious problem requiring you to stop as soon as safely possible.
answers.feedback: Correct! Red warning lights indicate serious problems — low oil pressure, engine overheating, brake system failure, charging failure — where continuing to drive can cause severe damage or become unsafe. Stop as soon as safely possible.

answers.text: A minor system is activated, like high beams or turn signals.
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Green or blue lights indicate that a minor system is activated (high beams, turn signals, cruise control). Red is reserved for serious problems requiring immediate attention.

answers.text: A reminder to schedule routine maintenance eventually.
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Amber or yellow lights indicate "attention needed soon" — like routine maintenance reminders or minor issues. Red means stop now because the situation is serious.

questions.text: When adjusting your side mirrors using the modern blind-spot method, you should:

answers.text: Position them so you can clearly see the side of your own car in each mirror.
answers.feedback: Incorrect. This is the OLD method and it leaves a large blind-spot gap. Seeing your own car is wasted mirror space — you already know where your car is.

answers.text: Position them so you cannot see the side of your own car in either mirror.
answers.feedback: Correct! Adjusting mirrors so you CANNOT see your own car widens your field of view and eliminates the blind-spot gap. A passing car will smoothly transition from your rearview mirror to your side mirror to your peripheral vision with no gap.

answers.text: Point them straight down toward the road surface.
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Mirrors should be aimed at the lane beside you — not at the road surface. Pointing them down shows you pavement, not the cars you need to see.

answers.text: Leave them in whatever position the previous driver set.
answers.feedback: Incorrect. If anyone else has driven the car, the mirrors are likely set for their eye position and height, not yours. Always re-adjust before you start driving.

questions.text: While driving on the highway, your red oil pressure warning light comes on. What should you do?

answers.text: Pull over safely as soon as possible and shut the engine off.
answers.feedback: Correct! A red oil pressure light means the engine is running without adequate lubrication. Metal-on-metal contact can destroy an engine within minutes. Pull over safely and shut off the engine — don't try to drive even a short distance.

answers.text: Speed up to get home faster before damage occurs.
answers.feedback: Incorrect — speeding up is actually the worst thing you can do. Higher RPMs without oil pressure accelerate engine destruction. Pull over and shut off the engine immediately.

answers.text: Ignore it — the light is probably malfunctioning.
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Never assume a red warning light is malfunctioning. Even if it is, the cost of verifying is far less than the cost of a destroyed engine (often $4,000-$8,000+). Always treat a red light as real.

answers.text: Wait until you get to your destination to check the oil.
answers.feedback: Incorrect. By the time you reach your destination, the engine could be permanently damaged or seized. Red oil pressure warnings require immediate action — pull over and shut off.

questions.text: According to Florida law, you must signal a turn for at least how many feet before you turn?

answers.text: 25 feet
answers.feedback: Incorrect. 25 feet is much too short — other drivers wouldn't have time to react. Florida requires 100 feet of continuous signal before turning.

answers.text: 50 feet
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Florida Statute 316.155 requires at least 100 feet of signaling before a turn — that's roughly 2-3 seconds at city speeds.

answers.text: 100 feet
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida law (F.S. 316.155) requires continuous signaling for at least the last 100 feet before a turn. This gives other drivers and pedestrians time to anticipate your action.

answers.text: 500 feet
answers.feedback: Incorrect. 500 feet is the distance for dimming high beams to oncoming traffic — not for turn signals. Turn signals require 100 feet in Florida.

questions.text: What is the correct order for setting up your driving position before starting a trip?

answers.text: Mirrors, seat, steering wheel, seatbelt
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Mirrors MUST come after the seat is in its final position — because mirror settings depend on your eye position. Adjusting mirrors first forces you to redo them after moving the seat.

answers.text: Seat, steering wheel, mirrors, seatbelt
answers.feedback: Correct! Seat first (to establish eye position), then steering wheel (to ensure safe airbag distance), then mirrors (based on final eye position), then seatbelt. Each step depends on the previous one.

answers.text: Seatbelt, mirrors, seat, steering wheel
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Putting on your seatbelt first is fine, but adjusting mirrors before the seat forces you to re-adjust them after moving. The correct sequence is seat → steering → mirrors → seatbelt.

answers.text: Steering wheel, seat, seatbelt, mirrors
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The steering wheel can't be properly positioned until after the seat is set — they're linked. Correct sequence: seat → steering wheel → mirrors → seatbelt.

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.2 Quiz — Starting, Steering, and Basic Maneuvers

questions.text: Which hand position on the steering wheel does the Florida Driver License Handbook currently recommend as the safest for drivers in vehicles with airbags?

answers.feedback: 10-and-2 is older guidance. It's no longer recommended because it puts forearms directly in the path of a deploying airbag, risking broken arms and facial injuries.

answers.text: 9-and-3
answers.feedback: Correct. 9-and-3 keeps your arms clear of the airbag housing and gives maximum steering control — the current Florida recommendation.
12-and-6 leaves almost no leverage on the wheel and isn't a real steering technique — it's how you hold a plate, not a steering wheel.

answers.text: One hand at 12 o'clock
answers.feedback: One-handed driving at 12 o'clock kills your reaction time and puts your arm directly in front of the airbag. Both hands belong on the wheel — at 9-and-3.

questions.text: You parallel-park on a street in Tallahassee facing downhill with a curb on your right. Which way should your front wheels be pointed?

answers.text: Straight ahead — no turning needed
answers.feedback: Straight wheels and gravity give a runaway car. Parked cars on a grade must always have their wheels turned.

answers.text: Turned left, away from the curb
answers.feedback: That's the uphill rule. On a downhill slope, you want wheels pointed at the curb so a rolling car is stopped by the curb.

answers.text: Turned right, toward the curb
answers.feedback: Correct. "Down to the curb." Wheels turned right mean that if the parking brake fails, the car rolls into the curb instead of into the street.

answers.text: Direction doesn't matter as long as the parking brake is on
answers.feedback: The parking brake is one layer of safety; wheel direction is another. Florida hill-parking procedure requires both.

questions.text: Under Florida law (F.S. 316.1945), what is the minimum distance you must keep between your parked vehicle and a fire hydrant?

answers.text: 5 feet
answers.feedback: 5 feet is far too close. Firefighters need room to connect hoses — any less than 15 feet blocks access.

answers.text: 10 feet
answers.feedback: Ten feet is a ticket in Florida. The legal minimum is 15 feet — remember the 15-20-30-50 pattern.

answers.text: 15 feet
answers.feedback: Correct. 15 feet from a fire hydrant. Pattern to lock in: 15 (hydrant), 20 (crosswalk), 30 (stop sign), 50 (railroad).

answers.text: 30 feet
answers.feedback: 30 feet is the rule for stop signs and traffic control devices, not fire hydrants. Hydrants are 15 feet.

questions.text: You want to make a U-turn at a Florida intersection. Under F.S. 316.1515 and F.S. 316.151, which of the following must ALL be true for the U-turn to be legal?

answers.text: There is a "U-Turn Permitted" sign posted
answers.feedback: Florida doesn't require a "U-Turn Permitted" sign. U-turns are legal by default unless a "No U-Turn" sign is posted and conditions are safe.

answers.text: No "No U-Turn" sign is posted, you have adequate sight distance, and you make the turn from the far-left lane
answers.feedback: Correct. All three conditions are required: no prohibition sign, safe visibility (typically 500 feet each way), and initiating the turn from the far-left lane.

answers.text: Traffic is light enough that you don't need to signal
answers.feedback: A signal is always required before any turn, including a U-turn. Light traffic doesn't waive the signaling rule.

answers.text: You're on an interstate highway at an exit ramp
answers.feedback: U-turns are never legal on interstate highways in Florida, including exit ramps. That's a serious ticket and a safety risk.

questions.text: What is the primary visual reference a driver should use when backing straight up?

answers.text: The rearview mirror only
answers.feedback: The rearview mirror has a narrow field of view and misses low-to-the-ground objects. It's a supporting tool, not the primary one.

answers.text: The backup camera, because it shows everything behind the car
answers.feedback: Backup cameras flatten motion and miss peripheral movement. They supplement your eyes — they don't replace the over-the-shoulder look.

answers.text: Looking over the right shoulder through the rear window, with mirrors and camera as support
answers.feedback: Correct. The over-the-right-shoulder look is the primary reference; mirrors and camera fill in what your direct view can't catch.

answers.text: Looking straight forward and relying on the side mirrors alone
answers.feedback: Looking forward means you can't see where you're going. Side mirrors alone leave a huge rear blind zone.

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.3 Quiz — Speed Management and Stopping Distances

questions.text: Total stopping distance — the complete distance needed to stop a moving vehicle after a hazard appears — is the sum of which two components?

answers.text: Braking distance + skid distance
answers.feedback: Skid distance is a type of braking distance under poor traction, but the formula is missing the reaction distance — the feet you travel before your foot hits the brake.

answers.text: Reaction distance + braking distance
answers.feedback: Correct. Total stopping distance = reaction distance (feet traveled while you perceive and react) + braking distance (feet traveled while the brakes bring you to a stop).

answers.text: Perception distance + tire friction distance
answers.feedback: "Perception distance" is another term sometimes used, but "tire friction distance" isn't a standard component. The correct two components are reaction distance and braking distance.

answers.text: Speed × reaction time, only
answers.feedback: That's only the reaction-distance component. You also have to add the braking distance — the feet the vehicle covers after the brakes engage.

questions.text: You're driving on a wet road at night. Using Florida's following distance guidance, what minimum gap should you keep between you and the vehicle ahead?

answers.text: 2 seconds
answers.feedback: 2 seconds is below even the ideal-conditions minimum. At highway speeds, 2 seconds puts you inside the car ahead's braking distance.

answers.text: 3 seconds
answers.feedback: 3 seconds is the baseline for ideal conditions only. Wet pavement and night driving each add a second.

answers.text: 5 seconds
answers.feedback: Correct. Start with the 3-second baseline, add 1 second for wet pavement and 1 second for night driving — a minimum of 5 seconds.

answers.text: 10 seconds
answers.feedback: 10 seconds is overkill and can disrupt traffic flow. The correct adjustment is 3 baseline + 1 wet + 1 night = 5 seconds.

questions.text: If you double your speed — say, from 30 mph to 60 mph — what happens to your vehicle's kinetic energy (the crash force at impact)?

answers.text: It stays about the same — mass is what matters, not speed.
answers.feedback: Both mass and velocity matter. At constant mass, the velocity-squared term in KE = ½mv² dominates — doubling speed quadruples energy.

answers.text: It doubles.
answers.feedback: Doubling is linear. Since velocity is squared in the KE formula, doubling speed gives you 2² = 4 times the energy — not 2×.

answers.text: It triples.
answers.feedback: Not quite. Doubling speed means the energy is multiplied by the speed ratio squared: (2)² = 4, so the energy quadruples.

answers.text: It quadruples — speed is squared in the KE formula.
answers.feedback: Correct. KE = ½ × m × v². Since velocity is squared, doubling speed quadruples the crash energy — which is why highway crashes are disproportionately severe.

questions.text: Under Florida law (F.S. 316.183), what is the default speed limit in a business or residential district when no speed limit sign is posted?

answers.text: 20 mph
answers.feedback: 20 mph is the Florida default for active school zones (when children are present or beacons flash), not residential or business districts.

answers.text: 25 mph
answers.feedback: 25 mph is common as a posted limit in many Florida cities, but the statewide default under F.S. 316.183 for business/residential districts is 30 mph.

answers.text: 30 mph
answers.feedback: Correct. Florida's default limit for business or residential districts is 30 mph when no sign is posted, under F.S. 316.183.

answers.text: 35 mph
answers.feedback: 35 mph is too high for unposted urban streets. Florida's business/residential default is 30 mph.

questions.text: You're driving 65 mph in a posted 65 mph zone during heavy fog that has dropped visibility to about 200 feet. A Florida trooper pulls you over. Can you legally be cited, and why?

answers.text: No — you were at the posted limit, which is always legal.
answers.feedback: Not true. Florida's Basic Speed Law treats the posted limit as the maximum under ideal conditions — not the legal speed in all conditions.

answers.text: Yes — Florida's Basic Speed Law (F.S. 316.183) requires a speed reasonable and prudent for conditions, regardless of the posted limit.
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.183 requires drivers to operate at a speed reasonable and prudent for current conditions. In dense fog, 65 mph is ticketable even with a 65 mph posted limit.

answers.text: No — speed citations only apply to vehicles exceeding the posted limit.
answers.feedback: False. Florida's Basic Speed Law covers speeding for conditions even when you're at or below the posted limit.

answers.text: Yes — but only if visibility drops below 100 feet.
answers.feedback: There is no fixed visibility threshold in the statute. The Basic Speed Law is a judgment standard: what's reasonable and prudent right now?

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.4 Quiz — Driving in Adverse Conditions

questions.text: Under Florida's Wipers On, Lights On law (F.S. 316.217), when are you required to turn on your headlights?

answers.text: Only at night, after sunset
answers.feedback: Headlights at night are a separate law. The Wipers On / Lights On rule applies any time wipers are running, day or night.

answers.text: Whenever your windshield wipers are in continuous use because of rain, smoke, or fog
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.217 requires headlights whenever your wipers are in continuous use. Daytime running lights don't count — your tail lights need to be on to be visible from behind.

answers.text: Only when visibility drops below 500 feet
answers.feedback: There's no 500-foot threshold for this rule. The trigger is whether your wipers are running, not a specific visibility number.

answers.text: Only if other drivers around you have their headlights on
answers.feedback: The law applies to you independently, regardless of what other drivers are doing. If your wipers are on because of weather, your headlights must be on.

questions.text: You enter dense fog while driving on a rural Florida highway. Which headlight setting is correct?

answers.text: High beams — you need more light to cut through the fog.
answers.feedback: High beams reflect off the fog's water droplets and create a wall of glare that reduces — not improves — your visibility.

answers.text: Low beams (and fog lights if equipped).
answers.feedback: Correct. Low beams aim under the fog; fog lights (if equipped) aim even lower and wider. This is both physics and Florida best practice.

answers.text: Parking lights only — easier on the eyes.
answers.feedback: Parking lights aren't bright enough to be seen by other drivers in fog, and they're not legal for driving in most conditions.

answers.text: Hazard lights only.
answers.feedback: Using hazard lights while driving is illegal in Florida and confuses drivers about your intentions. Use low beams, not hazards.

questions.text: You're driving in rain at night. Using the Florida adjustment rule, what is the minimum recommended following distance?

answers.text: 2 seconds
answers.feedback: 2 seconds is below even the dry-road minimum. At highway speeds, that's inside the car ahead's braking distance.

answers.text: 3 seconds
answers.feedback: 3 seconds is the baseline for ideal conditions only. Rain and night each add a second.

answers.text: 5 seconds
answers.feedback: Correct. 3 baseline + 1 for rain + 1 for night = 5 seconds minimum. Add another second for each additional factor like heavy traffic or fatigue.

answers.text: 10 seconds
answers.feedback: 10 seconds is excessive and disrupts traffic flow. The correct answer is 5 seconds based on the two stacked conditions.

questions.text: Your car begins hydroplaning at highway speed on a wet road. What is the correct response?

answers.text: Slam the brakes hard to stop immediately.
answers.feedback: Slamming the brakes during hydroplaning locks the tires and makes the skid worse. Hard braking is the number-one hydroplaning mistake.

answers.text: Steer sharply to one side to regain traction.
answers.feedback: A sudden steering input during hydroplaning can cause the car to spin out the moment tires regain traction. Keep the wheel straight.

answers.text: Ease off the accelerator, keep the steering wheel straight, and let the vehicle slow naturally.
answers.feedback: Correct. Ease off the accelerator, hold the wheel firmly straight, and allow the car to slow until the tires re-contact the road. Recovery usually takes 2–3 seconds.

answers.text: Pull the parking brake to force the tires to grip.
answers.feedback: The parking brake only locks the rear wheels and will almost certainly throw the car into a spin at highway speed.

questions.text: You approach a section of road covered by several inches of moving flood water. What should you do?

answers.text: Drive through at speed so water doesn't get into the engine.
answers.feedback: Driving fast through flood water pushes water into the engine and creates hydroplaning. Never drive through standing flood water at any speed.

answers.text: Drive through slowly to avoid creating a wave.
answers.feedback: 12 inches of water can float a car. You cannot see whether the road has collapsed underneath, and the current can sweep you off the road. Never drive through flooded roadway.

answers.text: Turn around and find an alternate route — 'Turn Around, Don't Drown.'
answers.feedback: Correct. 'Turn Around, Don't Drown' — the National Weather Service rule. Florida leads the nation in flood vehicle deaths and the reason is almost always underestimating water depth.

answers.text: Wait on the side of the road until someone else drives through first to prove it's safe.
answers.feedback: Another driver making it through doesn't prove it's safe — conditions change minute by minute in flooding, and trucks and SUVs can clear depths that sedans can't. Turn around.

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.5 Quiz — Vehicle Malfunctions and Emergency Procedures

questions.text: You experience a tire blowout while driving 65 mph on the interstate. What is the correct first response?

answers.text: Slam the brakes to stop as quickly as possible.
answers.feedback: Hard braking during a blowout shifts weight forward and makes the vehicle harder to control — it's the number-one blowout mistake.

answers.text: Grip the wheel firmly, ease off the accelerator, and let the car slow naturally before braking gently.
answers.feedback: Correct. Firm grip, foot off the gas, let the drag of the flat slow the car, then brake gently under 30 mph and pull to the shoulder.

answers.text: Yank the steering wheel sharply to counter the pull.
answers.feedback: A sharp steering input during a blowout causes oversteer and loss of control. Hold steady against the pull, don't fight it.

answers.text: Turn on hazards and continue at full speed to the next exit.
answers.feedback: Driving on a blown tire at full speed destroys the wheel and can cause a second failure. Slow immediately and pull off at the nearest safe location.

questions.text: Your brake pedal sinks to the floor and the car isn't slowing. Which combination of steps is correct?

answers.text: Turn off the ignition so the engine stops.
answers.feedback: Turning off the engine eliminates power steering and can lock the steering column in some vehicles. Keep it running and use engine braking.

answers.text: Yank the parking brake all the way up at once.
answers.feedback: A full yank of the parking brake at speed locks the rear wheels and can spin the car. Apply it gradually, in stages.

answers.text: Pump the pedal rapidly, downshift to a lower gear, and apply the parking brake gradually.
answers.feedback: Correct. Pumping can rebuild pressure in some failures, downshifting uses engine compression, and the parking brake is a backup — used gradually, never yanked.

answers.text: Steer sharply from side to side to scrub off speed.
answers.feedback: Sharp side-to-side steering creates instability without meaningful slowing, and it can hit other vehicles. Use engine braking and the parking brake instead.

questions.text: Your accelerator pedal sticks to the floor and the car keeps accelerating. What should you do first?

answers.text: Turn the engine off immediately, even while moving.
answers.feedback: Turning off the engine while moving loses power steering and power brakes — and some cars lock the steering column. Shift to Neutral first.

answers.text: Shift the transmission to Neutral, brake firmly, then turn off the engine only after stopping.
answers.feedback: Correct. Neutral disconnects the engine from the wheels. The engine revs harmlessly while you brake and steer to safety; shut down the engine only after stopping.

answers.text: Stomp repeatedly on the accelerator to free it.
answers.feedback: Stomping on the stuck pedal typically makes it worse. The real fix is disconnecting the engine from the wheels via Neutral.

answers.text: Drive toward the shoulder at speed until you run out of gas.
answers.feedback: Waiting to run out of gas is unacceptable — you have full control available by shifting to Neutral immediately.

questions.text: The rear of your car is sliding to the right during a wet-road skid, and the front is starting to point left. What is the correct recovery?

answers.text: Steer sharply LEFT to complete your intended direction.
answers.feedback: Steering further left worsens the skid. "Steer into the skid" means steer in the direction the rear is sliding — which brings the front back in line.

answers.text: Slam the brakes to stop the skid immediately.
answers.feedback: Hard braking during any skid locks the wheels and makes the skid worse. Ease off the gas and steer instead.

answers.text: Steer RIGHT — toward where the rear is sliding — and ease off the gas.
answers.feedback: Correct. Steer in the direction the rear is sliding (right) — that's where you want the front of the car to go. Ease off the gas at the same time.

answers.text: Accelerate hard to pull out of the skid.
answers.feedback: Accelerating during a rear-wheel skid usually worsens it. The universal answer is release the gas and steer toward where the front should go.

questions.text: Under Florida law (F.S. 316.065(1)), a driver must immediately give notice of a crash to law enforcement when anyone is injured or killed, or when apparent damage to any vehicle or other property is at least:

answers.feedback: Too low. F.S. 316.065(1) requires immediate notice to law enforcement at $2,000 in apparent damage (or any injury or death).
Too low. F.S. 316.065(1) requires immediate notice to law enforcement at $2,000 in apparent damage (or any injury or death).

Correct. F.S. 316.065(1) requires immediate notice to law enforcement when a crash results in injury or death, or apparent damage to any vehicle or other property of at least $2,000. If law enforcement does not complete a report of a crash that damaged a vehicle or other property, F.S. 316.066(1)(e) requires the driver to submit a written report (Form HSMV 90011S) to FLHSMV within 10 days — with no dollar minimum.
Too high. F.S. 316.065(1) sets the figure at $2,000 in apparent damage (or any injury or death).

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.6 Quiz — Vehicle Maintenance and Responsibility

questions.text: You perform the penny test on a tire. If Lincoln's ENTIRE head is visible above the tread, what does that mean?

answers.text: The tire has plenty of tread left and is safe.
answers.feedback: It's the opposite — visible Lincoln head means the tread is too shallow. The test passes when Lincoln's head is partially hidden by the tread.

answers.text: The tread is at or below 2/32 inch — the Florida legal minimum — and the tire must be replaced.
answers.feedback: Correct. The top of Lincoln's head sits at roughly 2/32 inch on a penny. If you can see his entire head, the tread is at or below Florida's legal minimum and the tire must be replaced.

answers.text: The tire passes the safety threshold but fails the legal threshold.
answers.feedback: Actually the reverse: the safety threshold (quarter test, 4/32") is higher than the legal threshold (penny test, 2/32"). A failed penny test fails both.

answers.text: The tire needs to be rotated to the rear axle.
answers.feedback: Rotation doesn't fix tread depth. A tire at or below 2/32" needs to be replaced — moving it to a different corner of the same car doesn't help.

questions.text: What is the MINIMUM auto insurance coverage Florida requires to register a vehicle?

answers.text: $10,000 Personal Injury Protection (PIP) and $10,000 Property Damage Liability (PDL).
answers.feedback: Correct. Florida requires $10,000 PIP and $10,000 PDL to register a vehicle. Bodily Injury Liability is NOT required for most drivers — but carrying it voluntarily is strongly recommended.

answers.text: $25,000 Bodily Injury and $50,000 Property Damage.
answers.feedback: Florida uniquely does NOT require Bodily Injury Liability from most drivers. The required minimums are $10K PIP and $10K PDL.

answers.text: $100,000 Comprehensive and $100,000 Collision.
answers.feedback: Comprehensive and Collision are optional coverages typically required only by lenders on financed vehicles. State minimums are $10K PIP and $10K PDL.

answers.text: No insurance is required in Florida because it is a no-fault state.
answers.feedback: Florida absolutely requires insurance to register a vehicle. "No-fault" refers to how claims are paid — not whether coverage is needed. $10K PIP and $10K PDL are the required minimums.

questions.text: Under Florida Statute 316.610 (Unsafe Vehicles), what authority does a Florida officer have?

answers.text: The officer can only issue a warning — no citations are allowed for equipment issues.
answers.feedback: F.S. 316.610 explicitly gives officers citation authority over defects affecting safe operation — not just warning authority.

answers.text: The officer can issue a citation and require the vehicle to be repaired before it is driven further when defects affect safe operation.
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.610 allows Florida officers to cite and order off-road status for vehicles with defects that affect safe operation — cracked windshields, bad headlights, unsafe tires, broken lights, etc. Repair can be required before further use.

answers.text: F.S. 316.610 applies only to commercial trucks and trailers.
answers.feedback: F.S. 316.610 applies to all vehicles on Florida roads — passenger cars, trucks, and trailers alike. It is not limited to commercial vehicles.

answers.text: The officer can cite the owner but never the driver.
answers.feedback: The operator of an unsafe vehicle can be cited directly under F.S. 316.610 — the statute is not owner-only.

questions.text: Industry guidance recommends replacing tires how often, regardless of tread depth?

answers.text: Every 2 years
answers.feedback: Two years is much more aggressive than industry recommendations. Most manufacturers and the rubber industry consensus point to 6 years.

answers.text: Every 6 years
answers.feedback: Correct. Tire rubber hardens and cracks with age. Manufacturers and industry groups recommend replacement every 6 years regardless of tread, with 10 years as an absolute maximum. The DOT code on the sidewall shows week and year of manufacture.

answers.text: Every 15 years
answers.feedback: 15 years far exceeds any safe threshold. Tire rubber deteriorates starting at about 6 years, with catastrophic failure risk rising after 10.

answers.text: Only when tread reaches the legal minimum — age does not matter.
answers.feedback: Age absolutely matters. Rubber degrades over time regardless of mileage — a low-mileage tire can still be unsafe if it's old.

questions.text: What is the typical recommended oil change interval for most modern passenger vehicles?

answers.text: 1,000 miles or once a month, whichever comes first.
answers.feedback: 1,000 miles is far more frequent than modern vehicles need. Modern oils and engines comfortably go 5,000+ miles between changes.

answers.text: 5,000 miles (or 5,000–7,500 depending on the manufacturer's recommendation).
answers.feedback: Correct. 5,000 miles is the common interval, with 5,000–7,500 being the range specified in most modern owner's manuals. Always follow the manufacturer's specific recommendation for your vehicle.

answers.text: 50,000 miles with modern oil.
answers.feedback: No passenger-vehicle manufacturer recommends 50,000-mile intervals. Even premium synthetic oils top out around 10,000–15,000 miles under ideal conditions.

answers.text: Only when the oil warning light turns on.
answers.feedback: The low-oil warning light means you've lost or burned oil — not that it's at the end of its service life. Waiting for that light to change oil leads to engine damage.

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.7 Knowledge Check — Parking and Backing Up

questions.text: When parallel parking, after pulling alongside the front car with rear bumpers roughly aligned, what is your next move?

answers.text: Back up straight first, then begin turning.
Begin backing slowly while turning the wheel sharply right (toward the curb) until the rear of your car is at approximately 45° to the curb.
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. From the aligned position, you back slowly while turning sharply toward the curb, aiming the rear of your car at the curb at roughly a 45° angle. Straighten the wheel when you reach that angle and continue backing until your front bumper clears the rear bumper of the car ahead.

answers.text: Turn the wheel sharply left and back up at speed.
Wait for the car ahead to move forward before backing.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. From the aligned starting position, the first move is to back slowly while turning the wheel sharply toward the curb (right, in a typical right-side parking situation). This swings the rear of your car into the space at about a 45° angle to the curb.

questions.text: When parking uphill with a curb on your right, which direction should your front wheels face?

answers.text: Toward the curb (right)
Away from the curb (left, toward the road)
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. Uphill with a curb: turn front wheels AWAY from the curb (to the left). If your brakes fail and the car rolls backward, the rear of the front tire catches on the curb and stops the car. Always also set the parking brake.

answers.text: Straight ahead
Wheel direction doesn't matter as long as the parking brake is set

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Uphill with a curb: turn the wheels AWAY from the curb (left, toward the road). If the car rolls backward, the rear of the front tire catches on the curb and stops the car. The reverse (downhill with curb) is wheels TOWARD the curb. Always set the parking brake in addition.

questions.text: In Florida, how close may you legally park to a fire hydrant?

answers.text: Within 5 feet is prohibited
Within 15 feet is prohibited
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. Florida Statute § 316.1945 prohibits parking within 15 feet of a fire hydrant. The space around a hydrant must remain clear so the fire department can connect hoses in an emergency.

answers.text: Within 30 feet is prohibited
There is no minimum distance

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida law prohibits parking within 15 feet of a fire hydrant (F.S. § 316.1945). The clearance lets the fire department connect hoses in an emergency. Violations result in tickets and frequent towing.

questions.text: What is the most important first step before backing any vehicle?

answers.text: Honk to alert anyone behind you.
Press the gas pedal lightly to test the engine.
Check all mirrors AND look over both shoulders before moving.
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. All mirrors plus both shoulder checks, every time. Backup cameras and mirrors have blind spots — there are objects directly behind your bumper that cameras and mirrors don't catch. Direct visual confirmation is the rule. Then back at idle speed.

answers.text: Rely on the backup camera — it shows everything behind you.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. The correct first step is to check all three mirrors AND look over both shoulders through the rear window. Backup cameras have blind spots — especially directly behind your bumper — and are a confirmation tool, not a replacement for direct visual checks. Honking and gas pedals don't keep small kids safe.

questions.text: When backing into a parking space, you should back until:

answers.text: Your rear bumper touches something to confirm you're in.
Your vehicle is straight and centered within the space, with the front bumper clearing the driving lane.
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. The goal is to be straight, centered between the lines, and far enough back that your front bumper is fully out of the driving lane. Anything less than that and you've blocked traffic or parked crooked.

answers.text: You feel the vehicle stop on its own.
Your rear wheels are over the curb at the back of the space.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Back until your vehicle is straight, centered between the lines, and your front bumper has cleared the driving lane. Don't aim to 'touch something' — that's how bumpers get dented. Aim for centered alignment and full clearance of the lane.

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.8 Knowledge Check — Nighttime and Low-Visibility Driving

questions.text: Under Florida law, when must your headlights be on?

answers.text: Only between midnight and 5 a.m.
Only when other vehicles are present
From sunset to sunrise AND whenever visibility is less than 1,000 feet
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. Florida F.S. § 316.217 requires headlights from sunset to sunrise AND whenever visibility is less than 1,000 feet (rain, fog, smoke, etc.). Florida also requires headlights whenever your windshield wipers are in continuous use due to precipitation.

answers.text: Only during heavy rain

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida F.S. § 316.217 requires headlights from sunset to sunrise AND whenever visibility is less than 1,000 feet due to weather. Also: whenever your wipers are in continuous use because of rain. Daytime running lights don't count — they don't light up the rear of your vehicle.

questions.text: Under Florida law, when should you dim your high beams for an oncoming vehicle?

answers.text: Within 100 feet
Within 500 feet
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. Florida F.S. § 316.238 requires you to dim within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle. The same statute requires dimming within 300 feet of a vehicle you're following (so your high beams don't reflect into their mirrors).

answers.text: Within 1,000 feet
Only if the oncoming driver flashes you

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida law requires dimming high beams within 500 feet of oncoming traffic. The follow-distance dim threshold is 300 feet. Until then, high beams give you the visibility you need on dark roads. Don't rely on the oncoming driver to flash you — dim proactively.

questions.text: What does 'overdriving your headlights' mean?

answers.text: Using high beams when you should be using low beams
Driving at a speed where your stopping distance is greater than the distance your headlights illuminate
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. If your headlights illuminate 200 feet ahead but your stopping distance is 270 feet, you cannot stop in time for anything that appears in the lit zone. The fix is to slow down until your stopping distance fits inside your visible distance. This is a real risk on unlit rural roads.

answers.text: Driving with too many headlights at once
Using fog lights when it's not foggy

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Overdriving your headlights means your stopping distance is greater than the distance your headlights illuminate — so you can't stop in time for anything that suddenly appears in the lit zone. The remedy is to slow down. On unlit roads with low beams, at 60 mph you're already overdriving them.

questions.text: When driving in fog, you should use:

answers.text: High beams to cut through the fog
Low beams only — high beams reflect off fog and reduce visibility further
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. High beams reflect off fog particles and create a wall of glare that makes visibility worse, not better. Low beams (or fog lights, aimed lower) cut through better. Also slow down significantly and increase following distance. Florida law (F.S. § 316.2397) generally prohibits using hazards while moving.

answers.text: Hazard lights while moving so other drivers can see you
No lights — they only make glare worse

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. In fog, use LOW beams only — high beams reflect off the fog particles and create a glare wall that worsens your visibility. Florida also prohibits using hazard lights while moving on most roads. Slow down, increase following distance, and consider pulling completely off if visibility drops to zero.

questions.text: Under Florida's GDL system, a 16-year-old driver with a Class E license may NOT drive between what hours without a licensed adult?

answers.text: 9:00 PM and 5:00 AM
10:00 PM and 4:00 AM
11:00 PM and 6:00 AM
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. Florida's GDL prohibits 16-year-olds from driving between 11:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m. unless accompanied by a licensed driver age 21+ or driving to/from work. For 17-year-olds, the window narrows to 1:00 a.m. – 5:00 a.m.

answers.text: Midnight and dawn

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida GDL: 16-year-olds may not drive between 11:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m. without a licensed driver 21+ (or for work). At 17, the restricted window narrows to 1 a.m. – 5 a.m. The restriction exists because about half of teen driving fatalities happen at night.

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.9 Knowledge Check — Seat Belts and Occupant Safety

questions.text: Under Florida law, who is legally responsible for ensuring all passengers under 18 are buckled?

answers.text: The passenger themselves
The driver
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. Under Florida F.S. § 316.614, the driver is responsible for ensuring all passengers under 18 are properly restrained — regardless of where they're sitting. If a 16-year-old in the back seat is unbelted, the driver gets the citation.

answers.text: Both equally — each gets their own ticket
Only a parent in the vehicle

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida law makes the driver legally responsible for all passengers under 18 — not the passengers themselves. If a 16-year-old in your back seat is unbelted, YOU get the ticket. 'Buckle up or get out' is reasonable, and it's on you as the driver to enforce it.

questions.text: Where should the lap belt portion of a seat belt be positioned?

answers.text: Across the stomach, just above the belly button
Across the hips and pelvis, not the stomach
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. The lap belt should sit across the hips and pelvis — bones that can take crash forces. Across the stomach or abdomen, the belt can cause severe internal injuries during a crash because soft tissue cannot absorb the same impact as the pelvis can.

answers.text: Across the upper thigh, near the knees
Above the rib cage

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. The lap belt belongs across the hips and pelvis — the strong pelvic bones can take crash forces. Across the stomach, the belt causes severe internal injuries in a crash because soft tissue can't absorb the impact like the pelvis can.

questions.text: What is the 'second collision' in a crash?

answers.text: The crash that happens after the first one, if cars behind don't stop
When the unbelted occupant's body strikes the interior of the vehicle after the car has stopped
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. The first collision is the vehicle hitting the object. The second collision — the one that injures or kills — is the occupant's body, still moving at the car's original speed by inertia, slamming into the dashboard, windshield, or another occupant. Seat belts prevent this by tying you to the car's deceleration.

answers.text: When airbags deploy and hit the driver
A second vehicle striking the wreckage

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. The 'second collision' is the unbelted occupant's body slamming into the car's interior after the car itself has stopped. This is the collision that actually injures and kills — your body is still moving at the original speed by inertia. Seat belts tie you to the car's deceleration so you stop with the car.

questions.text: How far should a driver sit from the steering wheel for safe air bag deployment?

answers.text: At least 4 inches
At least 10 inches
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. Sit at least 10 inches from the steering wheel (measured chest to wheel). Air bags deploy in about 1/20th of a second at speeds up to 200 mph — they are explosive devices, not soft pillows. Closer than 10 inches and the deploying bag can fracture your sternum or worse.

answers.text: As close as comfortable for control
Air bag distance doesn't matter — they're designed for any distance

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Sit at least 10 inches from the steering wheel — measured from your chest to the wheel. Air bags deploy at up to 200 mph in about 1/20th of a second. Closer than 10 inches and the bag itself becomes the injury source. Adjust your seat back and tilt the wheel to aim the bag at your chest, not your face.

questions.text: Florida's seat belt law is a 'primary enforcement' law. This means:

answers.text: Officers will only ticket seat belt violations if you're under 18.
Officers can stop you solely for not wearing a seat belt — no other violation is needed.
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. 'Primary enforcement' means the seat belt violation alone is enough to justify a traffic stop and citation. Florida F.S. § 316.614 is primary enforcement — an officer can pull you over and ticket you for the seat belt alone, with no other violation observed.

answers.text: You only have to wear a seat belt on primary highways.
The first violation is a warning; subsequent ones are tickets.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Primary enforcement = officers can stop you and ticket you for the seat belt violation alone, no other violation required. Some states have 'secondary' enforcement, where they need another reason to stop you. Florida is primary. Buckle up before you drive — every trip, every time.

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.10 Knowledge Check — What to Do After a Crash

questions.text: Under Florida law, what is required of any driver involved in a crash?

answers.text: You may leave the scene if the damage is minor.
You must stop at the scene — leaving is a criminal hit-and-run offense.
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. Florida F.S. §§ 316.061–316.063 require every driver involved in a crash to stop immediately at the scene. Leaving is a crime: misdemeanor for property damage, felony for injury, first-degree felony (with mandatory 4-year prison minimum) for death.

answers.text: You only need to stop if the other driver flags you down.
You must stop only if police arrive within 30 minutes.

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida law makes leaving the scene of ANY crash you're involved in a crime — even a parking-lot fender bender. The penalty escalates with severity: misdemeanor for property damage, felony for injury, first-degree felony with mandatory prison time for death. There is no version of 'drive away' that goes well.

questions.text: In Florida, when must you call 911 after a crash?

answers.text: Only if more than two cars are involved
Only if you suspect the other driver is at fault
When there is injury, death, or a vehicle cannot be moved under its own power
answers.feedback: Correct! F.S. § 316.065(1) requires the driver to immediately notify law enforcement when a crash results in injury or death, or apparent damage of at least $2,000. Under F.S. § 316.066(1)(a), law enforcement completes the crash report when there is injury, death, or a complaint of pain; a vehicle needs a wrecker; a commercial vehicle is involved; or DUI or leaving the scene is suspected. When in doubt, call. The dispatcher will determine whether units need to be sent.

answers.text: Never — you only need to call your insurance company

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida law requires reporting (calling 911) when there's injury, death, an undriveable vehicle, suspected impairment, or a commercial vehicle involved. The other answers are wrong: number of cars and fault assessment don't trigger the requirement. When in doubt, always call.

questions.text: You should NOT move an injured person after a crash unless:

answers.text: They ask to be moved
Help is more than 10 minutes away
There is immediate danger such as fire or rising water — moving them incorrectly can worsen spinal injuries
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. Moving an injured person with a possible spinal injury — gently or not — can paralyze or kill them. Wait for EMS, who have the training and equipment to immobilize the spine. The only exceptions are immediate, life-threatening dangers: fire, sinking, or being struck by other traffic.

answers.text: They have a minor cut

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Moving an injured person — especially someone with possible spinal injury — can paralyze or kill them. The only times to move them are: fire, sinking vehicle, or being about to be struck by other traffic. Otherwise, stay with them, keep them calm, and wait for EMS, who have the training and equipment to immobilize them safely.

questions.text: Which of the following must you exchange with the other driver after a crash?

answers.text: Just your phone number — insurance will handle the rest later
Name, driver's license number, insurance company and policy number, and license plate number
answers.feedback: Correct! Correct. You must exchange full identification and insurance information: name, address, driver's license number, license plate, vehicle description, and insurance company + policy number. Photographing each other's licenses and insurance cards is the easiest way to capture all of it accurately.

answers.text: Only insurance information — Florida doesn't require sharing your license
Only your insurance card; sharing your license is risky

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida (and every other state) requires drivers in a crash to exchange identification and insurance information: name, driver's license, plate, vehicle make/model, and insurance carrier + policy number. Phone numbers alone aren't enough. Photographing each other's licenses and insurance cards is the simplest way to capture all of it accurately.

questions.text: Under F.S. 316.066(1)(e), a Florida driver must submit a Driver Report of Traffic Crash (Self Report), Form HSMV 90011S, to FLHSMV when:

answers.text: Any crash occurs, regardless of damage
The crash caused damage to a vehicle or other property AND law enforcement did not complete a crash report — the report is due within 10 days after the crash
answers.feedback: Correct! F.S. § 316.066(1)(e): the driver of a vehicle that was in any manner involved in a crash resulting in damage to a vehicle or other property which does not require a law enforcement report must, within 10 days after the crash, submit a written report to the department on its approved form — the Driver Report of Traffic Crash (Self Report), Form HSMV 90011S. There is no minimum dollar amount. Submit it to SelfReportCrashes@flhsmv.gov or by mail to FLHSMV Crash Records.

answers.text: Only when both drivers agree to file
Only for crashes on Interstate highways

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. The driver's self-report (Form HSMV 90011S) is required under F.S. § 316.066(1)(e) when the crash damaged a vehicle or other property and law enforcement did not complete a crash report. It is due within 10 days after the crash, and there is no dollar threshold.

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.11 Knowledge Check — Costs & Insurance

questions.text: What is the legal minimum insurance coverage Florida requires for vehicle registration?

answers.text: $10,000 Personal Injury Protection (PIP) + $10,000 Property Damage Liability (PDL)
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida F.S. § 324 requires $10,000 PIP + $10,000 PDL as the legal minimum. Florida is one of only two states (with New Hampshire) that does NOT require Bodily Injury Liability by default. Most safety advisors strongly recommend buying more than the minimum.

answers.text: $25,000 Bodily Injury Liability + $50,000 PDL
$100,000 Bodily Injury Liability per person + $300,000 per crash
Florida has no minimum insurance requirement

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida's legal minimum is $10K PIP + $10K PDL. Bodily Injury Liability is NOT required by default in Florida — that's a famous gap in the law. Most advisors recommend adding BIL at $100K/$300K plus Uninsured Motorist coverage.

questions.text: In Florida's no-fault insurance system, who pays for your medical bills after a crash?

answers.text: Always the at-fault driver's insurance
Your own PIP coverage pays first, regardless of who caused the crash
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida's no-fault system means each driver's PIP pays their own medical bills up to $10,000, regardless of fault. PIP also covers your passengers, household members, and certain pedestrians. For costs above $10,000, you'd rely on your health insurance, Uninsured Motorist coverage, or pursuing the at-fault driver.

answers.text: The state of Florida from a public fund
Only your private health insurance, not auto insurance

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida is a no-fault state — your PIP pays first regardless of who caused the crash. There's no state public fund. The at-fault driver's BIL might come into play for very serious injuries, but PIP handles the first $10K of medical bills no matter what.

questions.text: What is the approximate AAA estimate of the true total cost of owning and operating an average new vehicle in Florida driven 15,000 miles a year?

answers.text: About $3,000–$4,000 per year (just gas and insurance)
About $5,000–$6,000 per year
About $11,000–$12,000 per year, or roughly $0.75–$0.80 per mile
answers.feedback: Correct! AAA's annual 'Your Driving Costs' study puts the average at roughly $11,000–$12,000/year for a new vehicle driven 15,000 miles annually. This includes fuel, insurance, depreciation, maintenance, registration, and loan interest — many of which new drivers underestimate.

answers.text: About $20,000–$25,000 per year

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. The true cost is closer to $11,000–$12,000/year — about $0.75–$0.80 per mile. Most drivers focus on the loan payment and forget insurance, fuel, maintenance, depreciation, and registration. Depreciation alone often exceeds $3,000/year on a new car.

questions.text: Why is Uninsured/Underinsured Motorist (UM/UIM) coverage especially valuable in Florida?

answers.text: It's required by Florida law
