Florida has one of the highest uninsured-driver rates in the country (around 20%), so the odds of being hit by an uninsured driver are significant
answers.feedback: Correct! Roughly 20% of Florida drivers are uninsured — one of the highest rates in the U.S. UM/UIM protects YOU when an uninsured or underinsured driver causes the crash. It's optional under Florida law but strongly recommended.

answers.text: It pays the at-fault driver's bills
It reduces your registration fees

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. UM/UIM is optional in Florida but strongly recommended because Florida has one of the highest uninsured-driver rates (~20%) in the country. It protects you when the at-fault driver has no insurance or not enough. It doesn't pay the other driver's bills — it pays yours.

questions.text: What is an SR-22?

answers.text: A type of supplemental insurance policy
A certificate of financial responsibility filed by your insurer with Florida DHSMV, typically required for 3 years after DUI or certain other violations
answers.feedback: Correct! An SR-22 is not insurance itself — it's a certificate filed by your insurance company with the Florida DHSMV proving you carry the required coverage. Required after a crash while uninsured, certain license suspensions, or habitual traffic offender status. After a DUI conviction Florida requires the higher-limit FR-44 instead ($100,000/$300,000 bodily injury and $50,000 property damage, F.S. 324.023). Typically required for 3 years; any lapse triggers license suspension.

answers.text: A Florida tax form
A rebate program for safe drivers

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. An SR-22 is a certificate of financial responsibility, not a policy. Your insurer files it with the DHSMV to prove you have the required coverage. It's typically required for 3 years after a DUI or similar violation, and any lapse during that period triggers immediate license suspension. Coverage with SR-22 typically costs 30–50% more than standard.

quizzes.title: Lesson 3.12 Knowledge Check — Road Skills Test Maneuvers

questions.text: On the Florida road skills test, what is the most common reason drivers fail?

answers.text: Driving too fast
Rolling stops at stop signs — slowing but not coming to a complete stop
answers.feedback: Correct! Rolling stops are explicitly the #1 reason people fail Florida's road test. Examiners are trained to fail any stop sign or red light where wheels don't fully stop. Always count to one with wheels stopped before proceeding — even when no traffic is visible.

answers.text: Hitting another car
Forgetting to fasten their seat belt

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Rolling stops are the most common road test failure. The examiner requires a COMPLETE stop — wheels not moving — at every stop sign and red light, even when there's no cross-traffic. Slowing but not stopping is an automatic failure on the Florida road test.

questions.text: What happens if you touch or mount a curb during parallel parking on the Florida road skills test?

answers.text: Nothing — gentle contact is permitted in parking
Automatic failure — curb contact during a maneuver is a listed 'dangerous action'
answers.feedback: Correct! Touching or mounting a curb during parking or a three-point turn is one of Florida's listed automatic-failure 'dangerous actions' on the road test. Examiners are strict — if you feel yourself getting close to a curb, pull forward and reset rather than continuing.

answers.text: Small deduction; you'll still pass
Only matters if the curb is painted yellow

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Curb contact during parking is an automatic failure on the Florida road test — a listed 'dangerous action.' Even a gentle bump fails the test. The safer approach: if you're close to the curb, pull forward and try again rather than continuing.

questions.text: Before starting the road test, the examiner does a pre-test vehicle safety check. What happens if a brake light is burned out?

answers.text: The examiner gives a warning and proceeds with the test
The test is cancelled, and you must reschedule with a compliant vehicle
answers.feedback: Correct! The examiner refuses to administer the test if the vehicle fails the safety check — lights, signals, horn, wipers, mirrors, seat belts, registration, insurance, or tag/decal. You'd have to reschedule. Always verify everything works the night before your test.

answers.text: It's only a deduction, not a cancellation
The examiner asks you to fix it on the spot

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. A burned-out brake light cancels the test — the examiner won't proceed with a non-compliant vehicle. Same for missing decal, expired registration, broken signal, missing insurance proof, etc. Verify the vehicle the night before to avoid wasting a test slot.

questions.text: Florida law requires drivers to signal at least how far in advance of a turn or lane change?

answers.text: 10 feet
50 feet
100 feet
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida F.S. § 316.155 requires signaling at least 100 feet before a turn or lane change (200 feet on highways). On the road test, late signals or no signals are common deduction reasons.

answers.text: 500 feet

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida F.S. § 316.155 requires a 100-foot signal minimum (200 ft at highway speeds). Late or missing signals are common road-test deductions. Build the habit of signaling well in advance, every time.

questions.text: Before you can take the Florida Class E road skills test, how many hours of supervised driving must you have completed (and how many at night)?

answers.text: 30 hours total, 5 at night
50 hours total, 10 at night
answers.feedback: Correct! Florida requires 50 hours of supervised driving — including at least 10 hours at night — before you can take the Class E road skills test. A parent or guardian certifies the hours on the application. Plus, you must have held the Learner's License for at least 12 months without traffic convictions.

answers.text: 75 hours total, 25 at night
100 hours total, 40 at night

questions.feedback_incorrect: Incorrect. Florida requires 50 hours of supervised driving (10 at night) before the road test. You also need to have held your Learner's License for at least 12 months without traffic convictions. Parent/guardian certifies the hours. This 50/10 requirement is one of the most effective safety measures in the GDL system.

quizzes.title: Unit 3 Summative Assessment — Vehicle Control and Handling

questions.text: Which foot should you use to operate BOTH the brake and accelerator pedals in a standard automatic-transmission vehicle?

answers.text: Left foot only — it's closer to the brake.
answers.feedback: Using only your left foot in an automatic is incorrect. The right foot handles both pedals, pivoting at the heel.

answers.text: Right foot for both pedals.
answers.feedback: Correct. Right foot on both pedals, pivoting at the heel. The left foot rests on the dead pedal.

answers.text: Left foot for brake, right foot for gas (two-footed driving).
answers.feedback: Two-footed driving leads to accidental brake-and-gas-at-once and inconsistent braking. Use the right foot for both.

answers.text: Either foot — it doesn't matter.
answers.feedback: It does matter. Standard technique is right foot only, pivoting between brake and gas.

questions.text: A RED warning light on your dashboard generally means:

answers.text: A minor issue you can address at your next service appointment.
answers.feedback: Red lights are NOT "wait until next service." Red = stop now. Yellow/amber = address soon.

answers.text: A serious issue requiring immediate attention — stop safely and check it.
answers.feedback: Correct. Red warning lights — battery, oil pressure, temperature, brake — indicate serious issues. Pull over safely and investigate before continuing.

answers.text: That a non-critical system is operating normally.
answers.feedback: Green indicators mean normal operation. Red means serious issue.

answers.text: Nothing specific — red lights are purely decorative.
answers.feedback: Dashboard lights are functional, not decorative. Red is the highest severity tier.

questions.text: Florida law (F.S. 316.155) requires turn signals to be activated at least how far BEFORE the turn or lane change?

answers.text: 25 feet
answers.feedback: 25 feet is too short — drivers behind you wouldn't have enough warning.

answers.text: 50 feet
answers.feedback: 50 feet is still short. Florida's minimum is 100 feet — about four car lengths.

answers.text: 100 feet
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.155 requires at least 100 feet of continuous signaling before a turn or lane change.

answers.text: 300 feet
answers.feedback: 300 feet exceeds the statute. The minimum is 100 feet — giving early signals earlier than 100 is fine but not legally required.

questions.text: When should you engage the parking brake?

answers.text: Only when parking on steep hills.
answers.feedback: Best practice is every time you park. Relying only on the transmission Park mechanism puts all the strain on a small internal pawl.

answers.text: Every time you park, regardless of terrain or transmission.
answers.feedback: Correct. Engage the parking brake every time. It backs up the transmission, prevents roll-away, and keeps the parking-brake mechanism from seizing from disuse.

answers.text: Only in manual-transmission vehicles.
answers.feedback: Parking brakes apply to both manual and automatic transmissions. Automatics benefit too — the Park pawl alone is fragile.

answers.text: Never — the transmission's Park position is sufficient.
answers.feedback: The Park pawl is a small internal part. Every time you use the parking brake, you spread the load and prevent a failure.

questions.text: What is the recommended hand position on the steering wheel for modern vehicles with airbags?

answers.text: 10 and 2 o'clock
answers.feedback: 10-and-2 is the older recommendation. With airbags, hands at 10-and-2 can be thrown into your face when the bag deploys. 9-and-3 is the modern standard.

answers.text: 9 and 3 o'clock
answers.feedback: Correct. 9-and-3 is the airbag-era standard — it keeps your hands clear of the airbag deployment path and gives you the best leverage for push-pull steering.

answers.text: 12 o'clock (both hands at the top)
answers.feedback: Hands at 12 put your arms directly in the airbag deployment path. This is unsafe.

answers.text: 6 o'clock (both hands at the bottom)
answers.feedback: Hands at 6 give almost no steering leverage and look relaxed but are dangerous in an emergency. Use 9-and-3.

questions.text: When backing up in a vehicle WITHOUT a backup camera, what is the recommended technique?

answers.text: Look only at the rearview mirror.
answers.feedback: The rearview mirror alone has significant blind spots directly behind the car, especially at the bumper level where a child or pet could be.

answers.text: Place right hand on passenger seat, turn head and shoulders to look out the rear window, and proceed slowly.
answers.feedback: Correct. Right hand on passenger seat, turn head and shoulders to look out the rear window directly, and back slowly. Use mirrors to supplement, not replace, direct vision.

answers.text: Look over your left shoulder only.
answers.feedback: Looking only over the left shoulder doesn't show the path directly behind the vehicle. Turn to look out the rear window instead.

answers.text: Back up at the same speed you drive forward.
answers.feedback: Reverse speed should always be much slower than forward speed. Backing is a limited-visibility maneuver.

questions.text: When you finish parallel parking, how far should your tires be from the curb?

answers.text: Touching the curb tightly.
answers.feedback: Touching the curb scuffs the sidewall and can knock the wheel out of alignment. Leave some clearance.

answers.text: No more than 12 inches (about one foot) from the curb.
answers.feedback: Correct. Florida's road test standard (and general good practice) is 12 inches or less from the curb. More than that means you're blocking traffic.

answers.text: 24 inches or more for safety clearance.
answers.feedback: 24 inches is too far — your car sticks into the travel lane. The standard is 12 inches or less.

answers.text: It doesn't matter as long as you're parallel.
answers.feedback: Distance matters. Too far from the curb blocks traffic; touching the curb damages the tire.

questions.text: Proper driving position places your chest at least how far from the steering wheel?

answers.text: 2 inches
answers.feedback: 2 inches is dangerously close — the airbag deploys at over 100 mph and could cause serious injury at that distance.

answers.text: 10 inches
answers.feedback: Correct. At least 10 inches from chest to steering wheel center gives the airbag room to deploy safely without injuring you.

answers.text: 24 inches
answers.feedback: 24 inches is typically too far — your arms would be straight and you wouldn't have proper steering leverage. 10 inches is the minimum; a normal bent-elbow posture gets you there naturally.

answers.text: It doesn't matter as long as you can reach the pedals.
answers.feedback: Distance matters because of airbag deployment. Too close, and the airbag injures the driver instead of protecting them.

questions.text: Total stopping distance is made up of which two components?

answers.text: Perception distance and decision distance.
answers.feedback: Perception and decision are both part of the reaction phase, but the standard model divides total stopping distance into REACTION distance and BRAKING distance.

answers.text: Reaction distance (time from seeing to braking) and braking distance (time from brake press to stop).
answers.feedback: Correct. Total stopping distance = reaction distance (while your foot moves to the brake) + braking distance (while the brakes slow the car). Both grow with speed — braking distance grows as the SQUARE of speed.

answers.text: Highway distance and surface-street distance.
answers.feedback: Road type doesn't define stopping distance components. The components are reaction and braking, regardless of road type.

answers.text: Tire distance and engine distance.
answers.feedback: Stopping distance components are reaction and braking, not mechanical parts.

questions.text: If you double your speed from 25 mph to 50 mph, how much does your kinetic energy (crash energy) increase?

answers.text: Doubles (2 times).
answers.feedback: Close, but the relationship is quadratic, not linear. Kinetic energy = ½mv² — doubling speed quadruples energy.

answers.text: Quadruples (4 times).
answers.feedback: Correct. KE = ½mv². Doubling v makes v² four times larger. Triple the speed would make crash energy 9× larger. This is why small speed increases produce massive crash damage.

answers.text: Stays the same.
answers.feedback: Energy absolutely depends on speed. Kinetic energy scales with the square of speed — doubling speed quadruples energy.

answers.text: Increases by 50%.
answers.feedback: 50% is far too small. Doubling speed quadruples crash energy — the quadratic nature of KE is why speed matters so much.

questions.text: The three-second rule is a technique for determining what?

answers.text: How long to wait at a stop sign.
answers.feedback: Stop-sign duration is "complete stop until safe to proceed," not a fixed count. The three-second rule is about following distance.

answers.text: Minimum safe following distance behind another vehicle.
answers.feedback: Correct. Pick a fixed point; when the vehicle ahead passes it, count "one-Mississippi, two-Mississippi, three-Mississippi." If you reach it before three, you're too close.

answers.text: How long turn signals must blink.
answers.feedback: Turn signals run on a distance standard (100 feet), not a time standard. The three-second rule is about following distance.

answers.text: The time you have to react to a skid.
answers.feedback: Skid reaction times are tighter than three seconds. The three-second rule is the minimum time gap you leave behind the vehicle ahead.

questions.text: Florida's default speed limit in a residential district when no sign is posted is:

answers.text: 20 mph
answers.feedback: 20 mph is Florida's business/school-zone default, not residential.

answers.text: 25 mph
answers.feedback: Many states use 25 for residential, but Florida's statutory default is 30 mph. Always follow any posted sign if present.

answers.text: 30 mph
answers.feedback: Correct. Florida's default residential speed limit is 30 mph per F.S. 316.183. Posted signs override the default.

answers.text: 35 mph
answers.feedback: 35 mph exceeds Florida's residential default. The statutory default is 30.

questions.text: The maximum posted speed limit on Florida's rural interstate highways is generally:

answers.text: 55 mph
answers.feedback: 55 mph is the F.S. 316.183(2) default wherever nothing is posted outside a business or residence district. A limited-access highway may be posted as high as 70 mph.

answers.text: 65 mph
answers.feedback: 65 mph is the most FDOT may post on a divided highway of four or more lanes outside an urban area of 5,000 or more (F.S. 316.187(2)(b)). On a limited-access highway the ceiling is 70 mph.

answers.text: 70 mph
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.187(2)(a) allows up to 70 mph on a limited-access highway, which is how Florida's rural interstates are posted. Always follow the actual posted sign — some segments are lower.

answers.text: 80 mph
answers.feedback: 80 mph is not legal on any Florida highway. The statutory maximum is 70 mph on rural interstates.

questions.text: Under Florida's Wipers On, Lights On law (F.S. 316.217), headlights are required whenever:

answers.text: It is after sunset.
answers.feedback: Headlights are required after sunset, but the Wipers On, Lights On law adds a DAY requirement: wipers in continuous use = headlights on.

answers.text: The windshield wipers are in continuous use because of rain, smoke, or fog.
answers.feedback: That's one of the two requirements — but the law also specifies that daytime running lights alone don't count because they don't activate tail lights. Both B and C are correct.

answers.text: Daytime running lights alone don't satisfy the law.
answers.feedback: That's one of two requirements. The other is that headlights must be on whenever wipers are in continuous use. Both B and C are correct.

answers.text: Both B and C are correct.
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.217 requires headlights whenever wipers are in continuous use (rain/fog/smoke), AND daytime running lights alone don't satisfy the law because they don't activate tail lights.

questions.text: Driving in dense fog, which headlight setting gives you the best visibility?

answers.text: High beams
answers.feedback: High beams reflect off water droplets in fog and create a blinding white wall. Low beams are correct.

answers.text: Low beams (and fog lights if equipped)
answers.feedback: Correct. Low beams aim under the fog layer and don't reflect glare back at you. Fog lights (if equipped) further improve the low-angle illumination.

answers.text: Parking lights only
answers.feedback: Parking lights give too little light to see the road ahead. Use low beams.

answers.text: Hazard lights only
answers.feedback: Hazards are for stopped or disabled vehicles, not moving ones in Florida. Use low beams while driving in fog.

questions.text: Your car begins to hydroplane on a wet interstate. What is the correct response?

answers.text: Slam the brakes hard to stop.
answers.feedback: Hard braking while hydroplaning locks the wheels. When the tires re-contact the road, you spin. Hands off the brake.

answers.text: Ease off the accelerator, keep the wheel straight, and let the car slow naturally until traction returns.
answers.feedback: Correct. Ease off the gas, hold the wheel straight at 9-and-3, and let the vehicle coast. Traction returns in 2–3 seconds as speed drops.

answers.text: Steer sharply to one side to regain traction.
answers.feedback: Sharp steering while hydroplaning causes a spin the instant tires grip again. Keep the wheel straight.

answers.text: Pull the parking brake.
answers.feedback: The parking brake locks the rear wheels and spins the car. Never apply it on a hydroplaning vehicle.

questions.text: Driving in rain at night, the minimum recommended following distance is:

answers.text: 2 seconds
answers.feedback: 2 seconds is below even the dry-road minimum. In rain and at night, you need more, not less.

answers.text: 3 seconds
answers.feedback: 3 seconds is the dry-road baseline. Rain and night each add 1 second: 3 + 1 + 1 = 5.

answers.text: 5 seconds (3 base + 1 rain + 1 night)
answers.feedback: Correct. Start at 3 (dry), add 1 for rain, add 1 for night. 5 seconds is the minimum. Add more for heavy traffic, large trucks, or fatigue.

answers.text: 10 seconds
answers.feedback: 10 seconds is excessive for just rain at night. Each adverse factor adds 1 second — 5 is the typical two-factor minimum.

questions.text: A tire blows out at highway speed. Your correct first response is to:

answers.text: Slam the brakes.
answers.feedback: Hard braking during a blowout shifts weight forward and makes the vehicle harder to control — the number-one blowout mistake.

answers.text: Grip the wheel firmly, ease off the accelerator, let the car slow naturally, then brake gently under 30 mph.
answers.feedback: Correct. Firm grip, foot off the gas, let the drag of the flat slow the car, then brake gently under 30 mph and pull to the shoulder.

answers.text: Yank the steering wheel hard to counter the pull.
answers.feedback: Yanking the wheel causes oversteer and loss of control. Hold steady against the pull.

answers.text: Maintain speed to the next exit.
answers.feedback: Driving on a blown tire at full speed destroys the wheel and risks a second failure. Slow immediately.

questions.text: Your accelerator is stuck and the car keeps accelerating. What should you do FIRST?

answers.text: Turn the ignition off immediately while moving.
answers.feedback: Shutting the engine off at speed loses power steering and power brakes, and some cars lock the steering column. Neutral first, off later.

answers.text: Shift the transmission to Neutral, then brake firmly, then turn off the engine only after stopping.
answers.feedback: Correct. Neutral disconnects the engine from the wheels — the runaway stops immediately and you keep power steering and power brakes. Engine off after you're safely stopped.

answers.text: Stomp on the stuck pedal to free it.
answers.feedback: Stomping is unreliable and can make it worse. Disconnect the engine from the wheels by shifting to Neutral.

answers.text: Aim for a soft object to crash into.
answers.feedback: Intentional crashing is a last resort after all real options are exhausted. Neutral-brake-steer comes first.

questions.text: In a rear-wheel skid where the rear of the car is sliding to the right, the correct steering response is to:

answers.text: Steer left (the direction you were trying to go).
answers.feedback: Steering further left worsens the angle of the skid. "Steer into the skid" = steer where the rear is sliding, so the front and rear align again.

answers.text: Steer right (into the direction the rear is sliding).
answers.feedback: Correct. Steer into the direction the rear is sliding (right here). Ease off the gas at the same time. Never brake hard during a skid.

answers.text: Brake hard and keep steering straight.
answers.feedback: Hard braking during a skid locks the wheels and worsens the slide. Ease off the gas and steer into the skid.

answers.text: Accelerate hard to pull out of the skid.
answers.feedback: Accelerating during a rear-wheel skid doesn't reliably correct it — in FWD cars it usually worsens oversteer. Steer, don't add power.

questions.text: Under F.S. 316.065(1), the driver of a vehicle involved in a crash must immediately notify law enforcement when the crash results in injury or death, or when apparent damage to any vehicle or other property is at least:

answers.feedback: $500 is below the statute. F.S. 316.065(1) sets the notice threshold at $2,000 in apparent damage.
$1,000 is below the statute. F.S. 316.065(1) sets the notice threshold at $2,000 in apparent damage.

Correct. F.S. 316.065(1) requires the driver to immediately, by the quickest means of communication, notify the local police, the county sheriff, or the Florida Highway Patrol when a crash results in injury or death, or apparent damage of at least $2,000. Separately, F.S. 316.066(1)(e) requires a written self-report to FLHSMV within 10 days for any crash with vehicle or property damage that law enforcement does not report — that report has no dollar threshold.
$5,000 is above the statute. F.S. 316.065(1) sets the notice threshold at $2,000 in apparent damage.

questions.text: Florida's legal minimum tire tread depth is:

answers.text: 2/32 inch (the penny test threshold)
answers.feedback: Correct. Florida's legal minimum is 2/32" — the height of Lincoln's head on a penny. If you can see his entire head when the penny is in the tread, the tire fails.

answers.text: 4/32 inch (the quarter test threshold)
answers.feedback: 4/32" is the safer recommended replacement point (quarter test), not the legal minimum. The legal minimum is 2/32".

answers.text: 6/32 inch
answers.feedback: 6/32" is closer to a new-tire depth, not a legal minimum. Florida's minimum is 2/32".

answers.text: Tire tread isn't regulated in Florida.
answers.feedback: Tire tread is regulated. A tire below 2/32" can be cited under the unsafe-vehicle statute (F.S. 316.610).

questions.text: Florida's minimum auto insurance requirements for registration are:

answers.feedback: Correct. Florida requires $10,000 Personal Injury Protection (PIP) and $10,000 Property Damage Liability (PDL). Bodily Injury Liability is NOT required for most drivers — though strongly recommended.
Florida uniquely does NOT require Bodily Injury Liability from most drivers. The statutory minimums are $10K PIP and $10K PDL.

answers.text: Full coverage — comprehensive and collision required
answers.feedback: Comprehensive and collision are optional — typically required only by lenders on financed vehicles. State minimums are $10K PIP and $10K PDL.

answers.text: No insurance required — Florida is no-fault
answers.feedback: Florida absolutely requires insurance to register a vehicle. "No-fault" refers to how claims are paid — not whether coverage is required.

questions.text: Florida Statute 316.610 covers:

answers.text: Speed limits in school zones.
answers.feedback: Speed limits are in F.S. 316.183, not 316.610.

answers.text: Officer authority to cite or require repair of unsafe vehicles with defects that affect safe operation.
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.610 authorizes Florida officers to cite and/or require repair of vehicles with defects that affect safe operation — cracked windshields, bad headlights, unsafe tires, broken lights, and similar.

answers.text: The age limit for driving a vehicle.
answers.feedback: Driver age is set by F.S. 322 licensing statutes, not 316.610.

answers.text: Pedestrian right-of-way rules.
answers.feedback: Pedestrian right-of-way is covered in F.S. 316.130, not 316.610.

questions.text: Industry guidance is to replace tires every how many years, regardless of tread depth?

answers.text: 2 years
answers.feedback: 2 years is more aggressive than industry recommendations. Consensus sits around 6 years.

answers.text: 6 years
answers.feedback: Correct. Rubber hardens and cracks with age. Manufacturers and industry groups recommend replacement at 6 years, with 10 years as an absolute maximum. The DOT code on the sidewall (week + year) shows when the tire was made.

answers.text: 12 years
answers.feedback: 12 years far exceeds safe limits. Tires over 10 years old are at high risk of failure.

answers.text: Age doesn't matter — only tread depth.
answers.feedback: Age matters independent of tread. Rubber degrades over time regardless of mileage.

quizzes.title: Lesson 4.1 Quiz — How Alcohol Affects the Body and Driving Ability

questions.text: Which of the following contains the SAME amount of pure ethanol as a 12 oz regular beer?

answers.text: One 1.5 oz shot of 80-proof liquor.
answers.feedback: Correct. One 12 oz beer (5% ABV), one 5 oz wine (12% ABV), and one 1.5 oz shot of 80-proof liquor (40% ABV) all contain approximately 0.6 fl oz of pure ethanol. The body treats them identically.

answers.text: One 16 oz bottle of wine.
answers.feedback: A standard wine serving is 5 oz — not 16 oz. A 16 oz bottle of wine contains roughly three standard drinks, not one.

answers.text: One 2 oz shot of rum.
answers.feedback: A 2 oz shot contains more ethanol than the 1.5 oz standard — roughly 1.3 standard drinks. The standard serving is 1.5 oz.

answers.text: One can of soda with a splash of whiskey.
answers.feedback: “A splash” is not a standard measurement. A standard drink of liquor is exactly 1.5 oz of 80-proof spirits. Mixed drinks often contain 2–3 standard drinks.

questions.text: Under Florida’s Zero Tolerance law (F.S. 322.2616), what BAC level will trigger automatic license suspension for a driver under the age of 21?

answers.text: .08 BAC or higher.
answers.feedback: .08 is the Florida per se limit for drivers 21 and older under F.S. 316.193. For drivers under 21, the Zero Tolerance threshold is much lower: .02.

answers.text: .02 BAC or higher.
answers.feedback: Correct. Under F.S. 322.2616, any driver under 21 with a BAC of .02 or higher faces automatic administrative license suspension. This is often less than one standard drink for most teens. The only safe amount under 21 is zero.

answers.text: .05 BAC or higher.
answers.feedback: .05 is not Florida’s zero-tolerance threshold. For under-21 drivers, the line is drawn at .02 BAC.

answers.text: .15 BAC or higher.
answers.feedback: .15 is where Florida ENHANCES DUI penalties for all drivers — but zero tolerance for teens kicks in far earlier, at .02.

questions.text: Approximately how quickly does a healthy liver eliminate alcohol from the bloodstream?

answers.text: About one standard drink per hour (~0.015% BAC per hour).
answers.feedback: Correct. The liver processes alcohol at a nearly fixed rate of about one standard drink per hour, dropping BAC by roughly 0.015% per hour. This rate cannot be sped up by any known method.

answers.text: About three drinks per hour.
answers.feedback: Three drinks per hour would be three times the actual rate. The liver can only process roughly one drink per hour — anything faster causes BAC to rise.

answers.text: At a rate that depends heavily on how much coffee or water you drink.
answers.feedback: Neither coffee nor water changes the liver’s elimination rate. This is one of the most dangerous myths about alcohol — only time works.

answers.text: Alcohol leaves the body almost instantly once you stop drinking.
answers.feedback: Alcohol does not leave the body instantly. At ~0.015% per hour, a .08 BAC takes about 5 hours to return to zero.

questions.text: Which driving ability does alcohol impair FIRST — typically before a drinker even realizes they’re affected?

answers.text: Muscle coordination — steering and braking movements.
answers.feedback: Muscle coordination is affected, but NOT first. Judgment is impaired before coordination, which is why drivers confidently take the keys when they shouldn’t.

answers.text: Judgment and self-awareness.
answers.feedback: Correct. Judgment is the first ability alcohol takes away — often before the drinker realizes they’re impaired. That’s why self-assessment is unreliable: the part of the brain doing the assessing is already impaired. Order is: judgment → vision → reaction time → coordination → consciousness.

answers.text: Consciousness — staying awake behind the wheel.
answers.feedback: Consciousness is the LAST ability to fail. By the time someone passes out drunk, every safety-related ability has been gone for a long time.

answers.text: Peripheral vision and eye tracking.
answers.feedback: Vision is affected early, but judgment is affected first. Judgment → vision → reaction time → coordination → consciousness.

questions.text: A friend at a party has been drinking and says a large coffee will sober him up enough to drive home. What’s the accurate response?

answers.text: Coffee will reduce his BAC by about half — it works as long as you drink enough of it.
answers.feedback: Coffee does NOT reduce BAC by any amount. It’s a stimulant — it makes an impaired person feel more awake without changing their actual impairment. This is one of the most dangerous driving myths.

answers.text: Coffee only masks drowsiness; it does NOT change BAC or impairment. The liver is the only route out, at ~0.015% per hour. He should not drive.
answers.feedback: Correct. Caffeine is a central nervous system stimulant that can reduce drowsiness, but it has zero effect on blood alcohol level. An impaired driver who feels more awake is still fully impaired — and arguably more dangerous because they feel confident. The liver eliminates alcohol at ~0.015%/hour, and that rate cannot be sped up.

answers.text: Coffee works, but only if combined with a cold shower.
answers.feedback: Cold showers are also a myth. Neither coffee nor a shower changes BAC. Only the liver’s fixed elimination rate (~0.015%/hour) removes alcohol from the body.

answers.text: Coffee is fine as long as he also eats some food.
answers.feedback: Food slows absorption only if eaten BEFORE or DURING drinking. Once alcohol is in the blood, food doesn’t remove it. The liver is the only elimination route.

quizzes.title: Lesson 4.2 Quiz — Drugs, Medications, and Driving Impairment

questions.text: A driver takes Benadryl for allergies before school and is pulled over weaving in her lane. Her breath alcohol reads .00. Under Florida law:

answers.text: She cannot be charged with DUI because her BAC is .00.
answers.feedback: Florida DUI does NOT require alcohol. F.S. 316.193 makes it illegal to drive with impaired normal faculties from ANY substance — alcohol, OTC, prescription, or illegal.

answers.text: She can still be charged with DUI under F.S. 316.193 because her normal faculties are impaired — regardless of what caused the impairment.
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.193 criminalizes driving while “normal faculties” are impaired, regardless of cause. Benadryl (diphenhydramine) is a sedating depressant, and the label explicitly warns against driving. A .00 breath reading doesn’t save the driver — the observed impairment does the prosecuting.

answers.text: She cannot be charged because Benadryl is sold over the counter.
answers.feedback: OTC status has no bearing on driving law. Legal purchase is not legal driving. The law cares about impairment, not where the substance came from.

answers.text: She can only be charged if the Benadryl was expired.
answers.feedback: Expiration date has no bearing on DUI. Benadryl impairs whether expired or not, and the law cares about impairment.

questions.text: Which of the following is a STIMULANT (speeds up the central nervous system)?

answers.text: Xanax (alprazolam)
answers.feedback: Xanax is a benzodiazepine, which is a DEPRESSANT. It slows the CNS, not speeds it up.

answers.text: Oxycodone
answers.feedback: Oxycodone is a NARCOTIC/opioid — a painkiller that heavily depresses the CNS. Not a stimulant.

answers.text: Adderall (amphetamine)
answers.feedback: Correct. Adderall (amphetamine) is a classic stimulant. Stimulants cause overconfidence, aggressive driving, and a sudden “crash phase” drowsiness as they wear off.

answers.text: LSD
answers.feedback: LSD is a HALLUCINOGEN — it distorts perception rather than speeding up the CNS.

questions.text: A driver holds a valid Florida medical marijuana card. After using cannabis at home, she drives and is pulled over for weaving. How does Florida law apply?

answers.text: The card exempts her from DUI charges.
answers.feedback: A medical marijuana card authorizes possession and use — not impaired driving. F.S. 316.193 has no medical-cannabis exemption.

answers.text: She can still be charged under F.S. 316.193 — Florida’s medical marijuana program does NOT exempt patients from impaired-driving laws.
answers.feedback: Correct. Florida’s medical marijuana program (administered by the Department of Health) gives legal possession and use, but does NOT exempt anyone from F.S. 316.193. Patients with valid cards are regularly convicted of DUI when their normal faculties are impaired.

answers.text: She can only be charged if she had more than 10 ng of THC.
answers.feedback: Florida has no “per se” THC threshold — impairment of normal faculties is what F.S. 316.193 measures, not a specific THC number.

answers.text: Florida has no DUI law for marijuana.
answers.feedback: Florida absolutely prosecutes marijuana DUIs under F.S. 316.193. The statute covers any substance that impairs normal faculties.

questions.text: What does it mean when two impairing substances have a “synergistic effect” on a driver?

answers.text: The two drugs cancel each other out, leaving the driver sober.
answers.feedback: Drugs do not “cancel out.” A depressant and a stimulant both impair; combining them doesn’t produce sobriety — it produces a driver who is impaired AND feels falsely alert.

answers.text: The combined impairment is greater than the sum of each drug’s individual effect — impairment multiplies rather than adds.
answers.feedback: Correct. Synergistic means the combined impairment exceeds the sum of individual effects — the classic example is alcohol + cannabis, which roughly produces 8× sober crash risk when each alone is around 2×. Two “small” doses can combine to produce complete impairment.

answers.text: The second drug reduces the first drug’s impairment.
answers.feedback: The opposite of synergistic. When drugs reduce each other, that’s called antagonism — and it’s not what happens with most recreational combinations.

answers.text: Only the stronger of the two drugs affects the driver.
answers.feedback: Both drugs affect the driver. Synergistic combinations compound rather than one masking the other.

questions.text: Under Florida’s implied consent law (F.S. 316.1932), by holding a Florida driver license a person has consented to which of the following?

answers.text: Breath testing only.
answers.feedback: Implied consent in Florida covers more than just breath. Since many drugs can’t be detected in breath, urine and blood testing are also covered.

answers.text: Breath, blood, and urine testing when lawfully requested by an officer; refusal triggers automatic license suspension and, under 2025’s Trenton’s Law, criminal penalties from the first refusal from the first refusal.
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.1932 covers breath, blood, and urine testing. Refusal triggers automatic administrative license suspension (1 year first, 18 months subsequent) and, under Trenton’s Law (effective October 1, 2025), refusing a breath test is now a criminal offense from the very first refusal (a second-degree misdemeanor; a first-degree misdemeanor on a second or subsequent refusal) in Florida.

answers.text: No testing — the Fifth Amendment protects all drivers from testing.
answers.feedback: The Supreme Court has repeatedly upheld implied-consent laws. By accepting a driver license, you’ve legally consented in advance to chemical testing when lawfully requested.

answers.text: Testing only if the driver has been drinking.
answers.feedback: Implied consent covers impaired driving from any substance, not just alcohol. Drugged-driving suspects are tested via blood or urine.

quizzes.title: Lesson 4.3 Quiz — Florida DUI Laws and Consequences

questions.text: Which of the following correctly matches Florida’s BAC thresholds to the driver category?

answers.text: .02 for under 21, .04 for CDL, .08 for adults 21+
answers.feedback: Correct. Florida uses three BAC thresholds: .02 for drivers under 21 (Zero Tolerance under F.S. 322.2616), .04 for commercial drivers (CDL, per F.S. and federal rules), and .08 for adults 21+ under F.S. 316.193. BAC of .15+ triggers enhanced penalties.

answers.text: .08 for all drivers regardless of age
answers.feedback: Florida has three different thresholds by driver category — not one universal limit. Drivers under 21 are .02 and CDL holders are .04.

answers.text: .05 for under 21, .08 for adults, .10 for CDL
answers.feedback: Close, but the numbers are wrong. Under 21 is .02 (not .05), CDL is .04 (not .10), adult is .08.

answers.text: .00 for under 21, .08 for adults, no CDL rule in Florida
answers.feedback: Under 21 is .02 (any detectable amount) — not .00. Florida also has a specific .04 CDL limit matching the federal standard.

questions.text: Under Florida’s DUI statute (F.S. 316.193), a driver can be charged with DUI even if the vehicle never moved. This is because the statute covers:

answers.text: Only drivers whose vehicles are actually moving.
answers.feedback: Florida law doesn’t require movement. The “actual physical control” standard specifically covers drivers who are capable of operating the vehicle even if it’s parked.

answers.text: “Actual physical control” of the vehicle — including sitting in the driver’s seat with keys in or near the ignition.
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.193 criminalizes driving OR being in actual physical control while impaired. If you’re in the driver’s seat with keys in or accessible near the ignition, you’re in physical control, even if the engine is off. Sleeping it off safely means moving to the back seat with keys away from reach — or waiting for a sober ride.

answers.text: Only drivers who have crashed or broken another traffic law.
answers.feedback: A crash or traffic violation is not required. Officers regularly arrest drivers sleeping in parked cars for DUI under the physical-control standard.

answers.text: Only drivers on public roads, never in parking lots.
answers.feedback: Florida DUI covers parking lots, private property with public access, and driveways too. Location isn’t a defense.

questions.text: At what point does a Florida DUI first become a FELONY?

answers.text: Every first-offense DUI is a felony.
answers.feedback: A first-offense DUI in Florida is a 2nd-degree misdemeanor, not a felony — but still carries jail, fines, license suspension, and a 75-year record.

answers.text: Second DUI within 5 years.
answers.feedback: A second DUI within 5 years triggers MANDATORY 10 days in jail, but remains a 1st-degree misdemeanor. The felony line is the third DUI within 10 years, any fourth DUI, or any DUI with serious injury or death.

answers.text: Third DUI within 10 years, any fourth DUI regardless of timing, or DUI causing serious bodily injury or death.
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.193 makes DUI a 3rd-degree felony on the third offense within 10 years or on any 4th offense regardless of timing. DUI with serious bodily injury is also a 3rd-degree felony, and DUI manslaughter is a 2nd-degree felony (1st-degree if the driver flees). Felony status means prison exposure, permanent record, and loss of voting/firearm rights.

answers.text: DUI is never a felony in Florida.
answers.feedback: Florida absolutely prosecutes DUIs as felonies. DUI manslaughter alone is a 2nd-degree felony with a 4-year mandatory minimum.

questions.text: Under Florida Statute 316.193(3)(c)3, DUI manslaughter carries which of the following consequences?

answers.text: Up to 6 months in jail and a small fine.
answers.feedback: Nothing close. DUI manslaughter is a 2nd-degree felony with a 4-year mandatory minimum — one of Florida’s most serious non-homicide offenses.

answers.text: Second-degree felony, up to 15 years prison, 4-year mandatory minimum, and permanent driver license revocation.
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.193(3)(c)3 makes DUI manslaughter a 2nd-degree felony: up to 15 years prison, $10,000 fine, 4-year mandatory minimum, and permanent driver license revocation. If the driver fled the scene, the offense escalates to a 1st-degree felony with up to 30 years. Insurance does NOT cover intentional acts, so civil liability stacks on top.

answers.text: Probation only if the driver has no prior record.
answers.feedback: The 4-year mandatory minimum prevents any probation-only resolution for DUI manslaughter, regardless of prior record.

answers.text: Mandatory life imprisonment.
answers.feedback: Life in prison is reserved for 1st-degree murder in Florida. DUI manslaughter caps at 15 years (or 30 if the driver fled), with a 4-year mandatory minimum.

questions.text: A realistic total cost for a typical first-offense DUI conviction in Florida (with no crash, no enhanced BAC) is closest to:

answers.text: $500 — just the statutory fine.
answers.feedback: The statutory fine is just one line of the bill. Real first-offense DUIs in Florida typically total 20x this amount once attorney, insurance, and court costs are counted.

answers.text: $1,500 — fine plus a short class.
answers.feedback: Still far below reality. FR-44 insurance alone typically adds ~$4,500 over three years; private DUI defense averages $3,500; court costs another ~$1,200.

answers.text: $10,000–$12,000 once you add attorney fees, FR-44 insurance jump, court costs, DUI school, interlock, towing, reinstatement fees, and lost wages.
answers.feedback: Correct. A typical first-offense Florida DUI totals around $10,000–$12,000 by the time you add attorney fees (~$3,500), FR-44 insurance premium jumps (~$4,500 over 3 years), court fines and fees (~$1,200), DUI school and substance-abuse evaluation (~$350), ignition interlock costs (~$600 when required), towing and impound (~$450), license reinstatement (~$235), and lost wages for court and class attendance (~$600). None of that includes civil damages from a crash.

answers.text: Free if the driver completes community service.
answers.feedback: Community service is typically required in ADDITION to fines, fees, insurance jumps, and the other costs. It doesn’t replace them.

quizzes.title: Lesson 4.4 Quiz — BAC and the Science of Impairment

questions.text: When does a drinker’s Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) typically reach its PEAK?

answers.text: While drinking the last drink.
answers.feedback: Absorption continues after swallowing stops. Most alcohol absorbs through the small intestine, which takes 30-90 minutes to reach full effect.

answers.text: 30 to 90 minutes AFTER the last drink.
answers.feedback: Correct. BAC typically peaks 30-90 minutes after the last drink because absorption from the small intestine continues after the drinking stops. This is why drivers who “feel fine” right after their last drink can hit peak BAC mid-drive — the rising-BAC pattern.

answers.text: 5 hours after the last drink.
answers.feedback: Too late. By 5 hours, the liver has eliminated ~0.075% BAC — the peak has already passed and you’re well down the elimination curve.

answers.text: BAC never peaks — it keeps rising until you stop drinking.
answers.feedback: BAC does peak. After the last drink, absorption completes within ~90 minutes and elimination takes over at ~0.015%/hour.

questions.text: A driver stops drinking at .12 BAC. Approximately how long will it take her to reach .00 BAC at the liver’s standard elimination rate?

answers.text: About 2 hours.
answers.feedback: The liver runs at a fixed ~0.015%/hour. From .12, two hours clears only ~0.03 BAC — still above .08 legal limit.

answers.text: About 4 hours.
answers.feedback: Four hours clears ~0.06 BAC. From .12 start, she’d be at ~.06 — still above the Zero Tolerance .02 line, and under 21 drivers are still legally impaired.

answers.text: About 8 hours (at ~0.015% BAC per hour).
answers.feedback: Correct. At 0.015%/hour elimination, .12 BAC requires .12 / .015 = 8 hours to reach .00. Nothing speeds this up — coffee, exercise, cold showers, and food have zero effect on the liver’s metabolism rate. Only time.

answers.text: About 24 hours.
answers.feedback: Too long. The liver processes ~0.015% BAC per hour consistently — .12 takes 8 hours, not 24.

questions.text: Which of the following can meaningfully speed up the liver’s elimination of alcohol?

answers.text: Strong coffee.
answers.feedback: Caffeine is a stimulant that reduces drowsiness — it has zero effect on the liver’s alcohol metabolism. “Coffee sober” is the most dangerous myth in impaired-driving culture: it produces a drunk driver who feels alert.

answers.text: A cold shower.
answers.feedback: Cold water changes nothing about liver metabolism. You end up with a cold, wet, still-impaired driver.

answers.text: Vigorous exercise.
answers.feedback: Exercise raises heart rate and burns calories but doesn’t speed up the liver’s alcohol metabolism. Only time works.

answers.text: None of the above — the liver eliminates alcohol at a fixed ~0.015% BAC per hour, and only time lowers BAC.
answers.feedback: Correct. The liver metabolizes alcohol at a biologically fixed rate of ~0.015% BAC per hour. Caffeine, cold showers, exercise, food, “sober up” pills, water, and willpower all have ZERO effect on that rate. Only time lowers BAC. This is why ride-sharing and waiting several hours are the only real answers after drinking.

questions.text: Two friends drink the same three standard drinks over the same hour. One ends up with BAC .05 and the other at BAC .10. The BIGGEST reason for this difference is typically:

answers.text: Body weight and biological sex.
answers.feedback: Correct. Body mass dilutes alcohol — more weight means lower BAC on the same drinks. Biological sex shifts BAC another 20-30%, because women on average have less body water and less stomach alcohol-dehydrogenase. Together these two factors explain most of the “same drinks, different BAC” gap. Food, drink pace, and drink strength follow behind.

answers.text: Which hand they held the glass in.
answers.feedback: Not a BAC factor. The six real drivers are body weight, biological sex, food, drink rate, drink strength, and time.

answers.text: Hair color.
answers.feedback: No connection. Body mass and sex are the dominant variables.

answers.text: Whether they wore a watch while drinking.
answers.feedback: No relationship. Weight and biological sex do the heavy lifting in this calculation.

questions.text: A driver is pulled over 15 minutes after leaving a bar and blows .075 on the roadside. At the station, 30 minutes later, a second breath test reads .09. What best explains the increase?

answers.text: The breathalyzer must be broken — BAC can’t rise after drinking stops.
answers.feedback: BAC absolutely rises after drinking stops — absorption continues for up to 90 minutes. Certified breathalyzers are routinely calibrated and their readings are legal evidence.

answers.text: BAC often continues rising for 30-90 minutes after the last drink (the rising-BAC pattern). Absorption isn’t complete when drinking stops, so the station reading captures a higher, still-rising BAC.
answers.feedback: Correct. Alcohol continues absorbing from the small intestine for 30-90 minutes after the last drink, so BAC keeps rising during that window. A driver at .075 roadside (15 min post-drink) is still on the rising curve and can easily be .09+ at the station retest. Florida prosecutors regularly convict drivers who were “under .08 at the roadside” using the station reading under F.S. 316.1932 implied consent.

answers.text: The driver must have had more alcohol between the two tests.
answers.feedback: Drivers in custody aren’t drinking. The rise is physiological — continued absorption toward peak BAC.

answers.text: The cold air at the station increased BAC.
answers.feedback: Temperature doesn’t raise BAC. Breathalyzers compensate for breath temperature internally.

quizzes.title: Lesson 4.5 Quiz — Peer Pressure and Refusal Strategies

questions.text: A friend keeps asking, every few minutes, if you’re “sure” you don’t want a ride with him after he’s been drinking. You’ve already said no twice. Which refusal strategy fits BEST for repeated, low-pressure asks?

answers.text: Over-explain your reasoning so he understands why you’re right.
answers.feedback: Over-explaining invites negotiation. Every new reason is something he can argue against. Short answers close the loop.

answers.text: Broken Record — repeat the same short “no thanks” each time without re-arguing the point.
answers.feedback: Correct. The Broken Record strategy is designed exactly for repeated low-pressure asks — you don’t have to win the argument, you just have to stay boring. “I’m good, thanks” five times in a row is more effective than one long speech because it gives him nothing to debate. Pressure dies on flat ground.

answers.text: Change your answer since he’s being persistent.
answers.feedback: Changing your answer under persistence trains friends to just ask harder next time. Your no has to hold.

answers.text: Start yelling so he stops asking.
answers.feedback: Escalating to a scene turns a quiet refusal into a fight. Keep it flat, repetitive, and boring — that’s what Broken Record is for.

questions.text: At a party, someone appears to have alcohol poisoning: cold skin, irregular breathing, unresponsive. You’ve been drinking too and are under 21. Under Florida’s overdose medical-assistance immunity law (F.S. 893.21), what protection does calling 911 in good faith give you?

answers.text: None — the statute protects only doctors, paramedics, and other medical professionals.
answers.feedback: Incorrect. F.S. 893.21 protects any person acting in good faith who seeks medical assistance — not just medical professionals.

answers.text: Protection from arrest, charge, prosecution, or penalty for the controlled-substance offences the statute lists — for the caller and for the person overdosing — but not for an underage-alcohol charge under s. 562.111
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 893.21(1) protects a person who in good faith seeks medical assistance for someone experiencing an alcohol-related or drug-related overdose, and F.S. 893.21(2) protects the person experiencing the overdose. Neither may be arrested, charged, prosecuted, or penalized for a violation of s. 893.132, s. 893.147(1), or s. 893.13(6) (excluding paragraph (c)) where the evidence came from seeking that help, and neither may be penalized for violating a condition of pretrial release, probation, or parole. The immunity is limited to those controlled-substance offences — it does not erase an underage-possession-of-alcohol charge under s. 562.111, and it does not cover DUI. Call anyway: a citation is survivable and an untreated overdose often is not. Put them in the recovery position and stay until EMS arrives.

answers.text: Complete immunity from every charge arising that night, including underage drinking and DUI.
answers.feedback: Incorrect. The immunity is limited to the controlled-substance offences F.S. 893.21 lists. It does not wipe out other charges such as underage possession of alcohol (s. 562.111) or DUI.

answers.text: Protection only if you are over 21.
answers.feedback: Incorrect. Age does not gate the immunity. F.S. 893.21(1) covers any good-faith caller, and F.S. 893.21(2) covers the person experiencing the overdose.

questions.text: You volunteered to be the designated sober driver for four friends. Partway through the night, two of them start pushing you to “just have one beer — you’ll be fine in an hour.” What’s the right call?

answers.text: Take the one beer — it’s just one, and you’re tall anyway.
answers.feedback: One standard drink is ~.02 BAC — already DUI under Florida’s Zero Tolerance law (F.S. 322.2616) if you’re under 21. “Tall” and “just one” don’t cancel the math.

answers.text: Flat no. A designated sober driver means .00 BAC — the entire promise collapses if you accept any drink, and your friends are trusting you with their lives.
answers.feedback: Correct. A designated sober driver means .00 BAC — full stop. The whole system collapses the moment you accept any drink, because your friends chose you based on zero drinks tonight. If the pressure keeps coming, use Broken Record: “I’m driving. Not tonight.” Repeat. The point of the DD role is it’s non-negotiable.

answers.text: Take a shot instead — shots are smaller than beers.
answers.feedback: A shot and a beer contain roughly the same alcohol (~0.6 oz ethanol per standard drink). Smaller glass doesn’t mean smaller BAC hit.

answers.text: Take one beer but drink it very slowly over an hour.
answers.feedback: Drinking slowly lowers peak BAC only slightly. The beer is still in your system, and as DD that’s a broken promise to the people counting on you.

questions.text: An intoxicated friend insists he’s driving home and is getting angry. You already have his keys. What’s the BEST approach?

answers.text: Give the keys back so he calms down.
answers.feedback: Returning keys to an impaired driver trades your momentary discomfort for someone else’s life. The anger will pass. A crash will not.

answers.text: Hold the keys, stay calm, pull in backup (another friend, a host, or a parent), and arrange a ride — don’t argue about whether he’s impaired.
answers.feedback: Correct. You don’t have to win the argument — you just have to keep him out of the driver’s seat. Pulling in a second person (host, parent, another friend, rideshare) spreads the pressure and the decision. Debating a drunk person about whether they’re drunk is a trap; they will out-stubborn you every time. Stay calm, stay firm, hold the keys, and get him a ride.

answers.text: Argue with him until he agrees he’s too drunk.
answers.feedback: Arguing with someone who’s impaired wastes time and almost never works — their judgment is exactly what’s compromised. Act calmly; don’t debate.

answers.text: Get in the passenger seat so he doesn’t drive alone.
answers.feedback: Riding with an impaired driver is never safer — you’re now a passenger in a high-risk vehicle. Stop the drive; don’t join it.

questions.text: You’re stranded at a party with an impaired ride, $0 in your bank account, and a parent who previously agreed to a “no-questions, no-consequences” pickup. What’s the correct move?

answers.text: Wait 3+ hours for your ride to sober up.
answers.feedback: Waiting to sober up assumes your ride stops drinking at a fixed time — which rarely happens at parties. Meanwhile, you’re one bad decision away from getting in the car.

answers.text: Text your parent — the no-questions pickup is exactly the safety net you pre-arranged for a night like this.
answers.feedback: Correct. The no-questions pickup is a pre-negotiated safety contract — you’re not “bothering” your parent, you’re using the system you both set up. Most parents would rather get a 1 AM pickup text than an ER call. This is part of the 4-part safety plan from the reading: ride app on your phone, a no-questions pickup, a backup sober friend, and $20 cash. The whole point is to remove “I had no other option” as an excuse before the night starts.

answers.text: Walk home, even if it’s 6 miles.
answers.feedback: Walking 6 miles at night — unlit roads, high-speed traffic, drunk drivers — isn’t a safe default. It’s a last resort, and a worse one than the no-questions pickup you already have.

answers.text: Ride with your impaired driver — you’re out of options.
answers.feedback: No-money and no-ride aren’t actually “out of options” — the no-questions parent pickup exists specifically to rule this option out. Never ride with an impaired driver.

quizzes.title: Lesson 4.6 Quiz — Alternatives to Impaired Driving

questions.text: Lesson 4.6 argues that a single-option ride home (“I’ll just Uber”) is fragile. What is the four-pillar plan it recommends instead?

answers.text: Uber, Lyft, taxi, and bus — four rideshare apps.
answers.feedback: Four versions of “someone else drives” is not what the lesson means by four pillars. The point is redundancy across different KINDS of support — if the rideshare app surges, the parent pickup still works.

answers.text: Rideshare + no-questions adult pickup + sober friend network + $20 cash fallback.
answers.feedback: Correct. The four pillars — rideshare, no-questions pickup, sober friend network, and $20 cash fallback — work because they fail independently. If surge pricing blows up the Uber budget, Pillar 2 (parent) or Pillar 3 (sober friend) covers you. If your phone dies, Pillar 4 (cash) keeps you alive. Any single-point plan breaks when its one point fails; the four-pillar plan is built so no single failure strands you.

answers.text: Drive yourself, ride with a friend, call a cab, or walk.
answers.feedback: “Drive yourself” is exactly the option this whole unit exists to remove. The four pillars all replace self-driving-impaired, never include it.

answers.text: One plan is enough if the plan is good.
answers.feedback: Single-point plans fail whenever their single point fails — dead phone, surge pricing, flaky friend. The redundancy is the entire point of the four-pillar design.

questions.text: When should the no-questions pickup agreement with a parent or trusted adult be negotiated?

answers.text: At 1 AM from the party, when you actually need it.
answers.feedback: Cold-pitching a sleeping parent at 1 AM is a terrible way to establish the agreement. The conversation has to happen before you need the infrastructure it creates.

answers.text: In daylight, sober, as a safety pact set up BEFORE you need it — so the decision to call is already made.
answers.feedback: Correct. The no-questions pickup is a pre-negotiated safety pact — set up in daylight, sober, with a specific script: “If I need a ride because I’ve been drinking or my ride has, can I call you without a lecture that night? We’ll talk the next day.” Most parents say yes because they’d rather pick you up at 1 AM than identify you at an ER. Having the agreement ahead means the decision to use it is already made — impaired you isn’t making the call, sober you already did.

answers.text: After you’ve already used it once, to explain yourself.
answers.feedback: Explaining after the fact skips the whole point. The agreement needs to exist so the call itself already has a rulebook — by the time you’re explaining it, the ride is over.

answers.text: It shouldn’t be discussed at all — parents already know to pick up.
answers.feedback: Parents may be willing to pick up, but without an explicit no-lecture-tonight agreement, fear of the consequence is what keeps teens from calling. The explicit pact is what removes that fear.

questions.text: Why does Lesson 4.6 argue that “I feel fine” is one of the LEAST reliable measurements of your own impairment?

answers.text: It’s actually pretty reliable — your body knows when it’s impaired.
answers.feedback: Self-reports are the least reliable impairment measurement in the literature. Every simulator study shows impaired drivers rating themselves near-normal while their actual driving performance has collapsed.

answers.text: The part of your brain that judges your own impairment is the same part being impaired by alcohol/drugs — which is why impaired drivers routinely rate themselves as “normal” at .08 in simulator studies.
answers.feedback: Correct. Alcohol impairs the prefrontal cortex — the brain region responsible for judgment and self-monitoring — BEFORE it impairs motor control. So the judgment being used to assess impairment is the judgment already compromised. This is why rules (“any drink = no driving”) beat self-assessment (“I feel fine, so I’ll drive”), and why pattern-interrupt tests (the subtract-7 test, key drop, “would I let this version of me drive my little cousin”) exist in the lesson: they force a real check past the “I feel fine” autopilot.

answers.text: Because everyone lies about it.
answers.feedback: Not lying — genuinely miscalibrated. Impaired people sincerely believe they’re fine, which is scarier than lying.

answers.text: Because alcohol has no effect on perception.
answers.feedback: Alcohol absolutely affects perception — including the perception of one’s own perception. That’s the whole problem.

questions.text: You’re hosting a small gathering. A guest has been drinking and is looking for their car keys to leave. Which set of actions BEST matches the host responsibilities in Lesson 4.6?

answers.text: Hand over the keys — they brought their own alcohol, so it’s not your legal problem.
answers.feedback: Social host liability in Florida can attach whether or not the host served the alcohol. Civil suits against negligent hosts regularly succeed when a visibly impaired guest is released and crashes. Whose bottle it was isn’t the line.

answers.text: Hold the keys, offer the couch rule (stay over), call an Uber or a parent pickup, and if anyone appears to be in medical trouble, call 911 — F.S. 893.21 gives the caller limited protection.
answers.feedback: Correct. The host responsibilities from the reading: collect/hold keys, enforce the couch rule (spare sleep spot), have rideshare queued up, don’t serve visibly impaired guests, and call 911 if anyone shows signs of alcohol poisoning (F.S. 893.21 protects the caller and the patient from the controlled-substance charges it lists, though not from an underage-alcohol charge). These are both the ethical AND legal positions — and they scale to any gathering size.

answers.text: Make them drive very carefully and take back roads.
answers.feedback: “Drive carefully” doesn’t unimpair anyone. Impaired reaction time and judgment don’t improve with back roads — they just change where the crash happens.

answers.text: Drive them home yourself regardless of whether you’ve been drinking.
answers.feedback: If YOU are sober, licensed, and your guest’s ride home is within your reach, that’s an option. But never drive a guest if you’ve been drinking yourself — now you’re the impaired driver.

questions.text: A classmate complains that Uber rides home “are expensive — $20 really adds up.” Using the cost figures from Lessons 4.3 and 4.6, roughly how many $20-$25 rideshare trips equal the all-in cost of a first-offense Florida DUI?

answers.text: About 10 rideshares.
answers.feedback: Too low. 10 rides at $25 is $250 — nowhere near a $10-12K DUI total.

answers.text: About 50 rideshares.
answers.feedback: Still too low. 50 rides at $25 is $1,250 — about 1/10th of a DUI’s all-in cost.

answers.text: About 400-500 rideshares (because a first FL DUI is ~$10-12K all-in).
answers.feedback: Correct. A first-offense Florida DUI runs roughly $10,000-$12,000 when you sum: fine (~$1,200), lawyer (~$3,500), DUI school (~$350), ignition interlock (~$600), FR-44 high-risk insurance (~$4,500/year for 3 years), tow + reinstatement + lost wages. Divided by $20-$25 rideshares, that’s 400-500 rides. “Uber is expensive” collapses as an argument by roughly a factor of 500 once you run the actual numbers.

answers.text: They’re about the same cost.
answers.feedback: Not remotely close. A $20 rideshare and a $10-12K DUI are three orders of magnitude apart.

quizzes.title: Unit 4 Summative Assessment — Alcohol, Drugs, and Impaired Driving

questions.text: Which of the following are all roughly ONE standard drink (about 0.6 oz of pure ethanol each)?

answers.text: 12 oz regular beer (~5% ABV), 5 oz wine (~12% ABV), 1.5 oz 80-proof liquor.
answers.feedback: Correct. The U.S. standard drink is 0.6 oz of pure ethanol — equivalent to 12 oz of 5% beer, 5 oz of 12% wine, or 1.5 oz of 80-proof liquor. Real-world pours at parties are often 2-3x this.

answers.text: 24 oz beer, 12 oz wine, 3 oz liquor.
answers.feedback: These are all 2-3x a standard drink. A 24 oz “tall” beer is closer to 2 standard drinks.

answers.text: Any amount of beer is one drink no matter the size.
answers.feedback: Volume matters. A 12 oz and a 24 oz beer contain different amounts of ethanol, which is what drives BAC.

answers.text: One shot, one glass, one can — regardless of volume.
answers.feedback: “One glass” is a social count, not a BAC count. Standard drinks are measured in ethanol oz, not container count.

questions.text: Alcohol is classified pharmacologically as a central-nervous-system depressant. Which of these is the FIRST ability typically impaired, well before obvious motor-skill failure?

answers.text: Leg strength.
answers.feedback: Muscle coordination goes later. The prefrontal cortex — judgment — goes first, often at BAC .02-.03.

answers.text: Judgment and risk assessment (prefrontal-cortex functions).
answers.feedback: Correct. The prefrontal cortex — responsible for judgment, risk assessment, impulse control, and self-monitoring — is the MOST alcohol-sensitive region of the brain. This is why the first thing an impaired driver loses is the ability to recognize they’re impaired. Motor coordination degrades later.

answers.text: Sense of smell.
answers.feedback: Smell doesn’t track alcohol impairment the way judgment does. The prefrontal cortex is the early-loss region.

answers.text: Hair color perception.
answers.feedback: Alcohol doesn’t affect color perception in that way. Judgment is the early-loss function.

questions.text: Developmental neuroscience shows the prefrontal cortex — the judgment center — isn’t fully mature until around what age?

answers.text: Age 13.
answers.feedback: Too early. Neuroimaging shows prefrontal development continues well past the teen years.

answers.text: Age 18.
answers.feedback: Legal adulthood at 18 doesn’t match neurological maturity — the prefrontal cortex keeps developing for several more years.

answers.text: Roughly age 25.
answers.feedback: Correct. Research using longitudinal MRI shows the prefrontal cortex continues to myelinate and refine connections until roughly age 25. This is part of why teens are biologically more vulnerable to alcohol-impaired decision-making — the judgment hardware is still under construction.

answers.text: Age 40.
answers.feedback: Too late. Core structural maturation wraps up by the mid-20s, though refinement continues subtly.

questions.text: Under Florida’s Zero Tolerance Law (F.S. 322.2616), a driver under 21 can lose their license for driving with what BAC?

answers.text: .08 or higher only.
answers.feedback: .08 is the adult per se DUI limit. For under-21 drivers, Florida’s Zero Tolerance line is much lower — .02.

answers.text: .02 or higher.
answers.feedback: Correct. Under F.S. 322.2616, an under-21 driver with BAC of .02 or higher faces automatic license suspension — 6 months for a first offense, 1 year for a second. One standard drink can put a smaller teen at or near .02. This is why the only safe rule if you’re under 21 is zero drinks before driving, period.

answers.text: Any detectable amount above .00.
answers.feedback: Florida’s statute uses .02, not “any detectable amount.” That small buffer exists because breathalyzers have margin of error.

answers.text: .05 or higher.
answers.feedback: .05 is not the under-21 line in Florida. The statute sets it at .02.

questions.text: Can a driver be charged with DUI in Florida for impairment caused by a legal over-the-counter medication like a first-generation antihistamine (e.g., diphenhydramine/Benadryl)?

answers.text: No — DUI only applies to alcohol and illegal drugs.
answers.feedback: Florida’s DUI statute (F.S. 316.193) explicitly covers impairment from alcohol OR any “chemical or controlled substance.” Legality of the substance is not a defense.

answers.text: Yes — Florida’s DUI law covers impairment from ANY substance, including legal OTC and prescription meds, under F.S. 316.193.
answers.feedback: Correct. Florida’s DUI law (F.S. 316.193) criminalizes driving with “normal faculties” impaired by ANY impairing substance — alcohol, illegal drugs, prescription meds, or OTC meds. First-generation antihistamines like Benadryl can cause significant drowsiness and impairment. The legal status of the drug is irrelevant to the DUI charge if impairment is proven.

answers.text: Only if combined with alcohol.
answers.feedback: Combination increases risk and can escalate charges, but impairment from OTC alone is sufficient for DUI in Florida.

answers.text: Only if the label specifically says “do not drive.”
answers.feedback: The warning label isn’t the legal trigger — actual impairment is. Many impairing meds carry no explicit no-drive warning.

questions.text: A classmate argues that stimulants like Adderall (without a prescription) make you a “better driver” because they make you more alert. Which statement is most accurate?

answers.text: He’s right — stimulants improve reaction time and driving.
answers.feedback: Stimulants don’t make safer drivers. Alertness without judgment produces confident, risk-taking impaired drivers — objectively higher crash risk.

answers.text: Stimulants cause overconfidence, risk-taking, and tunnel vision, and non-prescribed use is a federal felony plus a Florida DUI risk — “more awake” is not “safer.”
answers.feedback: Correct. Amphetamines/Adderall produce tunnel vision, overconfidence, impulsive lane changes, and aggressive driving — documented in driving simulator research. Non-prescribed Adderall is a Schedule II federal felony, and impairment from it triggers Florida DUI under F.S. 316.193. “Alert” is not the same as “safe.”

answers.text: He’s right only if he’s been sleep-deprived.
answers.feedback: The correct answer to sleep deprivation is sleep, not stimulants. Stimulants mask tiredness without fixing the impairment.

answers.text: He’s right if he only takes a small amount.
answers.feedback: Dose matters, but even small non-prescribed doses carry felony legal risk and measurable driving impairment.

questions.text: A driver with a valid Florida medical marijuana card is stopped and shows signs of impairment. Does the medical card prevent a DUI charge?

answers.text: Yes — the card is a legal exemption from DUI for marijuana.
answers.feedback: Medical authorization covers possession and use, not driving while impaired. Legal-to-use and legal-to-drive are separate questions.

answers.text: No — a medical marijuana card authorizes possession and use but does NOT exempt a driver from DUI if their normal faculties are impaired. F.S. 316.193 applies regardless.
answers.feedback: Correct. A Florida medical marijuana card authorizes possession and use but provides NO exemption from DUI prosecution under F.S. 316.193. The state must show the driver’s normal faculties were impaired — which is established through driving observations, field sobriety tests, and chemical tests. “But I’m a medical patient” is not a defense against impaired driving.

answers.text: Yes, as long as the THC level is below the legal limit.
answers.feedback: Florida does not have a per se THC level for DUI — impairment is established through observation and testing, not a threshold number.

answers.text: Yes, only on weekends.
answers.feedback: DUI law applies every day. Day of the week is not a defense.

questions.text: What does a “synergistic effect” mean when a driver combines alcohol with another depressant like an opioid pain med or a sleep aid?

answers.text: The two substances cancel each other out.
answers.feedback: The opposite — depressants amplify, not cancel. Alcohol + opioid is a leading cause of respiratory failure deaths.

answers.text: The combined impairment is simply the sum of each drug’s effect.
answers.feedback: Synergy is more than additive. Two depressants don’t stack 1+1=2 — they produce 1+1=3 (or higher) impairment.

answers.text: The combined impairment is MULTIPLIED — the total effect is significantly greater than the sum of the individual effects.
answers.feedback: Correct. Synergistic means the combined effect is multiplicatively greater than the sum of the individual effects. A person who could handle one beer fine and one sleeping pill fine may become severely impaired — or hospitalized — from the combination. Alcohol + opioids is a common cause of fatal respiratory depression. This is why warning labels say “do not use with alcohol.”

answers.text: There is no combined effect.
answers.feedback: There is definitely a combined effect — a dangerous one. Synergy is established pharmacology.

questions.text: Which set correctly lists Florida’s three primary per se BAC thresholds: Under 21 / CDL / Adult non-commercial?

answers.feedback: Correct. Under 21 = .02 (F.S. 322.2616 Zero Tolerance), CDL = .04 (F.S. 316.193), adult non-commercial = .08 (F.S. 316.193). Three different lines, three different populations. All are per se thresholds — at or above the line is DUI regardless of observable impairment.
These aren’t Florida’s numbers. Correct: .02 / .04 / .08.
Florida uses three different BAC thresholds depending on driver category — not a flat .08.
Close to Zero Tolerance for under 21 (.02) but wrong for CDL and adult non-commercial.

questions.text: A driver at .12 BAC crawls into his parked car’s driver seat to “sleep it off.” Keys are in the ignition but the engine is off. Can he be charged with DUI in Florida?

answers.text: No — the car wasn’t moving.
answers.feedback: Motion is not required. Florida’s statute covers “actual physical control,” which includes a driver with the ability to operate the vehicle.

answers.text: Yes — Florida’s DUI statute (F.S. 316.193) covers driving OR being in “actual physical control” of a vehicle while impaired. Driver seat + keys in ignition qualifies.
answers.feedback: Correct. F.S. 316.193 covers driving OR being in “actual physical control” of a vehicle while impaired. Florida courts have consistently held that being in the driver seat with immediate access to the keys satisfies physical control — even if the engine is off. If sleeping off impairment is the plan, the back seat with keys stashed out of reach is far safer than the driver seat.

answers.text: No — sleeping-it-off is explicitly protected by Florida law.
answers.feedback: Florida does not protect sleeping-it-off in the driver seat. That’s a persistent myth.

answers.text: Only if someone else reports him.
answers.feedback: An officer who observes the situation can establish physical control on their own.

questions.text: Under Florida law, a DUI becomes a FELONY (rather than a misdemeanor) in which of these situations?

answers.text: Any second-offense DUI.
answers.feedback: A second DUI in Florida is still a misdemeanor (with stiffer penalties). Felony status kicks in at the third-within-10-years trigger or with injury/death.

answers.text: Third DUI within 10 years, OR any fourth DUI, OR any DUI causing serious bodily injury or death.
answers.feedback: Correct. Under F.S. 316.193, the felony triggers are: (1) third DUI within 10 years of a prior, (2) any fourth or subsequent DUI regardless of time span, or (3) any DUI causing serious bodily injury (3rd-degree felony) or death (DUI manslaughter, 2nd-degree felony). All other repeat DUIs are still misdemeanors — serious, but misdemeanors.

answers.text: Only when a death occurs.
answers.feedback: Death is one trigger (DUI manslaughter) but not the only one. Priors and serious injury also elevate the charge.

answers.text: Only when BAC is above .15.
answers.feedback: BAC at .15+ triggers enhanced misdemeanor penalties, not felony status on its own.

questions.text: In Florida, DUI Manslaughter (F.S. 316.193(3)(c)3) is classified as a second-degree felony. What are the main penalties?

answers.text: Up to 6 months jail and a $500 fine.
answers.feedback: That’s roughly a first-offense misdemeanor DUI. Manslaughter is a second-degree felony — a much heavier charge.
